ideaData.title: Wound-field claw-pole BSG instead of permanent-magnet BSG on the inline-six
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: many premium 48 V belt machines (e.g. the belt-driven PM-synchronous motor-generator on Toyota Hilux 48V) use an interior-permanent-magnet rotor carrying roughly 0.35-0.45 kg of sintered NdFeB (N42SH/N38UH class, Dy-bearing for 150-180 °C under-bonnet duty). At belt ratio ~2.8:1 the machine reaches ~18,000 rpm, where PM back-EMF exceeds the 48 V system limit (ISO 21780 upper limit 60 V; 70 V transient), so the inverter must hold an active short circuit or field-weaken continuously on any fault, and the system carries over-voltage clamps and ASIL-rated fault reaction. Proposal: a Lundell (wound-field claw-pole) synchronous machine as in the Valeo iBSG (claw-pole, >65 Nm, 10 kWp motoring, 15 kWp regen). The rotor is two forged C10/C15 claw halves plus a ~0.25 kg copper field coil fed via slip rings and two brushes from a small field H-bridge on the inverter board. Because the EMF is proportional to field current, cutting the field de-excites the machine within ~0.1-0.2 s (field time constant) — no uncontrolled generation at overspeed, no magnet-temperature derating, and zero rare earth. The trade is efficiency: claw-pole peak ~85% (Valeo figure) vs ~90-92% for IPM, worth an estimated 0.5-1 g CO2/km in WLTP, which must be priced against fleet-CO2 targets.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes 0.35-0.45 kg NdFeB (€24-32 at €65-75/kg incl. coating), the Dy price exposure, magnet insertion/gluing and magnetisation; simplifies inverter over-voltage protection. Adds field coil copper, slip-ring/brush set and a field driver (€8-10). Claw forgings replace a laminated IPM stack at similar cost.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Rotor line changes from lamination stacking + magnet insertion + post-magnetisation to claw forging, coil winding on a bobbin and rotor press-fit/brazed slip-ring assembly — a mature alternator process with high-volume suppliers. No magnet storage/handling safety zone; balancing as today.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Rotor part count rises slightly (two claw halves, coil, bobbin, slip-ring, brush holder) but all are commodity alternator parts with automated assembly. Brush holder is a serviceable item accessible from the rear cover; no strong-magnet handling risk during service or rotor removal.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — rare-earth deletion and simpler fault protection, partly offset by brushes and efficiency loss
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Magnet deletion €24-32 + over-voltage protection simplification €2-4 = €26-36; minus field coil, slip-ring/brushes and field driver €8-10 and a CO2-compliance cost allowance of €4 → net €14-22 per vehicle × 50,000 = €0.70M-1.10M.

ideaData.riskNotes: Brush/slip-ring wear over 15 years/300,000 km with frequent start-stop and boost must be proven (endurance per LV 124/ISO 16750-4 thermal plus brush wear test). Lower efficiency costs CO2 and recuperation energy; claw-pole torque ripple and whine need NVH sign-off. Field time constant limits torque response for boost: validate tip-in drivability.

How this differs: Applies the rare-earth-free claw-pole topology to a luxury inline-six where PM belt machines are the alternative, and books the over-voltage-protection simplification and the CO2 penalty explicitly.

That carrier duplicates what the transmission already provides: a precise, stiff, ATF-wetted bore. Proposal: shrink-fit the stator (~180-260 mm OD lamination stack) directly into a machined seat in the transmission intermediate housing (bell-housing to main-case adapter), interference ~0.10-0.15 mm at 150 °C fit temperature, anti-rotation by two keys. Cooling switches from water jacket to ATF: a moulded PA66-GF30 spray ring fed from the 8HP lubrication circuit drips ATF over both end windings (~2-4 l/min). At 48 V the machine's continuous losses are modest (~0.6-1.2 kW at the rated point), which an ATF flow of 3 l/min removes with a ~10-15 K oil temperature rise; the existing transmission oil cooler is resized ~10-15%. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the motor carrier casting and its machining (€18-26), water-jacket core, coolant spigots/hoses/clips and LT-loop tee (€6-9), and two large O-rings (€1-2). Adds spray ring, ATF cooler capacity and bore machining in the transmission housing (€6-9).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Transmission plant adds a stator shrink-fit station (induction heating of housing to ~150 °C, ~60-90 s) and machines one more precision bore on the intermediate housing; motor supplier delivers stator and rotor as components. One coolant leak-test and hose installation removed from the vehicle line.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count down by the carrier, 2 hoses, 4 clips and 2 seals; the stator is located by the housing bore with a key for phase-lead orientation (poka-yoke). Service: stator replacement means transmission disassembly — acceptable for a part with no wear mechanism.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — removes a duplicated housing and a coolant branch on P2 variants
costSavingPotential.percentage: 10-16% of the P2 motor module cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Carrier €18-26 + coolant spigots/hoses/tee €6-9 + O-rings €1-2 = €25-37; minus spray ring, ATF cooler upsizing and bore machining €6-9 → €19-28 per vehicle, assuming all 50,000 MHEV use the P2 machine; × 50,000 = €0.95M-1.40M (scale by the P2 share if P0 variants remain).

ideaData.riskNotes: Shrink fit must hold torque reaction over −40 to 150 °C (Al housing expands faster than steel stack): calculate residual interference at hot, verify with torque-slip test. ATF ageing from varnish/enamel extractables and copper exposure — ATF compatibility test. Winding temperature at hot ATF (120-130 °C) and tow duty to be validated on dyno; NVH of stator in a thinner wall.

title: One BSG part number across petrol, diesel I6 and I4, pulley-only variants

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Supplier runs one line configuration (no stack-length or housing changeover); engine plant receives one machine and fits the variant pulley at engine dress — one extra pick-to-light station. Housing die count drops from 2-3 to 1.
ideaData.dfmDfa: One connector, one mounting pattern on the engine side via adapter, one torque spec. Poka-yoke on pulley variant by diameter-coded fixture and vision check; service carries one machine plus pulleys.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — volume pricing and avoided validation, low technical risk
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Volume price step 4-5% × €250-320 = €10-16 per unit; avoided DV/PV and software releases €2.5M-4M over 5 yrs = €0.5M-0.8M/yr ÷ 50,000 = €10-16 per vehicle, taken at 25% realisation for overlap with existing programme budgets = €2.5-4; minus pulley/bracket variant handling €0.5-1 → €12-19 per vehicle × 50,000 = €0.60M-0.95M.

ideaData.riskNotes: Compromise sizing: the diesel may need cooling margin the petrol does not (tow at 3,500 kg). Validate the worst-case duty (diesel tow, hot-ambient crawl) per ISO 16750-4 and LV 124 on the common machine; machine overspeed on the petrol with the smallest pulley must stay within rotor burst margin.

ideaData.title: FEAD geometry cancels BSG belt hub load, keeping the carry-over crank nose
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: when a 48 V belt machine is added, the crank pulley carries much higher span tensions than with a 12 V alternator — the drive span to the BSG reaches ~2,800-3,200 N during cranking/boost (≈ 65 Nm machine torque on a ~58 mm pulley at a 5:1 tight/slack ratio) and the opposite span during regen. Programmes then often upgrade the crank front end: larger crank nose diameter or a 42CrMo4 instead of C38 microalloyed crank forging grade, a reinforced #1 main bearing shell and a larger front oil seal. The hub load on the crank is the vector sum of the two spans leaving the crank pulley: F_hub = √(T1² + T2² + 2·T1·T2·cos φ), where φ is the angle between the two span directions (φ = 180° − wrap). With a typical 160-180° crank wrap the two spans leave the pulley almost parallel, so their forces add nearly colinearly (F_hub ≈ T1 + T2). Proposal: lay out the FEAD so the BSG is the first component after the crank in the motoring direction and the dual-arm tensioner and an idler set the crank wrap to ~120-130°, increasing φ to ~50-60° so the span forces partly cancel: F_hub falls ~12-20% at the peak case. Combined with orienting the resultant toward the stiffer main bearing cap direction, this keeps the carry-over crank nose, C38 forging grade, standard #1 main shell and front seal from the non-hybrid engine.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Avoids crank material/geometry upgrade (€3-5), reinforced front main bearing shell (€0.5-1) and larger front seal/cover machining (€1-2); keeps one crank part number across MHEV and non-MHEV engines (commonisation). Adds one idler (€2-3) if the layout requires it.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: No change on the crank line (carry-over part); front cover casting carries an extra idler boss if needed. FEAD bracket tooling designed once with the BSG. Belt-drive simulation and rig validation replace a crank redesign programme.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Crank and front-seal parts stay common with the non-hybrid engine, reducing part numbers and service variants. Layout keeps a single serpentine belt with one tensioner and easy belt routing label on the front cover.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — avoided upgrade cost plus crank commonisation
costSavingPotential.percentage: 3-6% of the crankshaft and front-end cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Avoided crank upgrade €3-5 + main shell €0.5-1 + seal/cover €1-2 = €4.5-8; minus idler €2-3 (only if needed; taken at 50% probability = €1-1.5) → €3.5-6.5, rounded to €3-6 per vehicle × 50,000 = €0.15M-0.30M.

ideaData.riskNotes: Lower crank wrap reduces belt traction at the crank: check crank pulley slip at the cold-crank and peak-regen cases (Euler-Eytelwein with wedge factor). Crank front-end fatigue and #1 main bearing load must be confirmed by multibody engine simulation and dyno durability with BSG duty cycles; belt span vibration and squeal tests.

title: Belt starter-generator mounted high on the front end, above the 900 mm wading line
timeToImplement: 18-24 months (aligned with an engine front-end update)
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Deletes the sealed/immersion-proof BSG variant premium (€6-10), splash shield and fixings (€3-5) and breather snorkel (€2-3), and cuts water-ingress warranty; adds longer belt and one idler (€3-5). Baseline: inherited front-end accessory drive layouts put the generator low on the block (often below the crank centreline on the exhaust or intake side). With a 900 mm wading requirement (Defender 110 figure) a low-mounted 48 V machine is immersed and its belt throws water: the BSG then needs a sealed variant (IP6K9K plus immersion, sealed brush or bearing cover, potted electronics), a splash shield, a breather snorkel routed up to the plenum and an anti-water-ingress belt-slip strategy. Proposal: re-lay the FEAD so the BSG sits on the top position (e.g. above the coolant pump, near the cam-cover line), with the machine connector and breather above wading height and the tensioner pivot on the BSG housing. Toyota did exactly this on Land Cruiser Hybrid 48V and Hilux 48V: the motor-generator is positioned high on the engine block so the 700 mm wading depth is preserved (Hilux can stop at that depth for 10 minutes). Belt length grows ~150-250 mm and one idler may be added; the 48 V phase/DC cables also shorten if the battery DC-link route runs along the top. Remaining wet parts (idlers, crank pulley) are standard.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: inherited front-end accessory drive layouts put the generator low on the block (often below the crank centreline on the exhaust or intake side). Proposal: re-lay the FEAD so the BSG sits on the top position (e.g. above the coolant pump, near the cam-cover line), with the machine connector and breather above wading height and the tensioner pivot on the BSG housing. Toyota did exactly this on Land Cruiser Hybrid 48V and Hilux 48V: the motor-generator is positioned high on the engine block so the 700 mm wading depth is preserved (Hilux can stop at that depth for 10 minutes). Belt length grows ~150-250 mm and one idler may be added; the 48 V phase/DC cables also shorten if the battery DC-link route runs along the top. Remaining wet parts (idlers, crank pulley) are standard.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the sealed/immersion-proof BSG variant premium (€6-10), splash shield and fixings (€3-5) and breather snorkel (€2-3), and cuts water-ingress warranty; adds longer belt and one idler (€3-5).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Engine dress sequence changes (BSG fitted from above, better robot access); bracket tool changes once. No new capex beyond FEAD bracket tooling (~€0.3-0.5M) and belt-drive validation.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Top-mounted BSG is serviceable from the engine bay without lifting the vehicle; fewer seals and shields to fit; belt route remains a single serpentine. Connector access improved for diagnostics.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — removes the wading-specific variant and warranty exposure on an off-road-capable SUV
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Sealed-variant premium €6-10 + splash shield €3-5 + snorkel €2-3 + water-ingress warranty reduction €1-2 = €12-20; minus longer belt and idler €3-5 → €9-15 per vehicle × 50,000 = €0.45M-0.75M.

ideaData.riskNotes: Top position is hotter (turbo/exhaust proximity on the hot side): check BSG electronics junction temperature with heat shielding per ISO 16750-4. Longer belt raises span vibration — run belt dynamics simulation and squeal tests. Wading validation at 900 mm, 7 km/h bow-wave and stationary immersion must pass with the standard machine.
ideaData.timeToImplement: 18-24 months (aligned with an engine front-end update)

How this differs: Applies the high-mount principle to a 900 mm wading luxury SUV and books the deleted sealing/shielding content.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: some 48 V P2 machines between the I6 and the 8-speed automatic (the Mazda M Hybrid Boost class: 12.4 kW, 153 Nm) are derived from traction practice — a distributed integer-slot winding (e.g. 48-72 slots) in a large-diameter, axially short stator. In such a pancake machine (OD ~250-280 mm, active length ~35-50 mm) the distributed end-turn overhang is as long as the active iron, so 40-55% of the copper does no torque work. Proposal: fractional-slot winding, 24 slots with 20 or 28 rotor poles (winding factor 0.966 for 24/20), built from 24 separate bonded-lamination T-segments. Each segment is wound off-line on a PA66-GF30 or PPS bobbin by a flyer winder (fill 60-70% with compacted wire), the 24 wound segments are rolled into a ring and shrink-fitted into the carrier. The overhang shrinks to about one segment width, cutting copper mass ~25-35% at equal current density. Because the P2 turns only at engine speed (800-6,500 rpm), the extra MMF space harmonics and rotor eddy losses of this layout stay modest. Large thin rings blanked from coil strip leave the centre as scrap (utilisation ~35-45% at 260 mm OD); T-segments nest in strip at ~70-80%. The result is a cheaper pancake stator for the bell-housing position, not a new motor concept.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Copper reduced 25-35% (~0.6-1.0 kg on a P2, €6-10); lamination utilisation up from ~35-45% (large thin ring) to ~70-80% for segments (€4-7); winding fully automated, no hairpin/insertion line (€3-5).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Tooth-segment progressive die and bonded-stacking, 2-4 parallel bobbin winders (cycle ~10-15 s per tooth), ring-forming and shrink fit; capex ~€4-6M vs a distributed-winding insertion line. Phase connection via a moulded busbar ring with welded coil ends.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Each tooth coil is testable before assembly (resistance, surge), so scrap is one tooth, not a stator. Busbar ring with coded positions prevents phase mix-up; segment keys orient the stack.

ideaData.riskNotes: Concentrated windings increase rotor eddy losses and torque ripple — check magnet temperature and NVH (engine-borne order masking helps) on dyno. title: One dual-arm pendulum tensioner on the BSG face replaces two single-arm tensioners
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Deletes one complete tensioner (€12-18), its bracket (€3-5) and one idler/pulley; the dual-arm unit costs €6-9 more than a single-arm unit. Module delivery removes one engine-dress operation. Baseline: because a BSG reverses the belt's tight side (motoring during crank/boost, generating during regen), early belt alternator-starter drives used two tensioners — one on each BSG span — or a mechanical tensioner plus a hydraulic strut, each with its own die-cast bracket, pulley and bolting (the "dual tensioner" BAS drive is a patented baseline layout). Proposal: one dual-arm pendulum tensioner whose two arms, each carrying a 70 mm idler, pivot on a common ring concentric with the BSG shaft and are coupled by one arc spring. When torque reverses, the whole arm pair swings around the BSG to keep the slack side loaded; the patent literature (pendulum-type double-arm tensioner) describes exactly this for 48 V drives where torque direction flips between cranking/boost and regen. Mount the ring directly on the BSG front end-shield (three M8 bosses cast into the housing), so the BSG + tensioner arrive as one pre-tested module. Toyota Land Cruiser Hybrid 48V uses a dual-arm tensioner on its aramid-reinforced belt for NVH and rough-road durability. Damping: asymmetric friction damper at the pivot (~20-30% damping ratio) to suppress span flutter at firing frequency.

title: 48 V P2 runs on HF-injection plus back-EMF observer; resolver and its harness deleted

Baseline: a 48 V P2 IPM motor in the bell-housing typically carries a variable-reluctance resolver (stator ring on the housing, lobed rotor target on the rotor carrier), a 6-wire shielded harness to the inverter and a resolver-to-digital excitation/demodulation stage on the inverter board — the same position-sensing chain as an 800 V traction motor, which must meet ASIL C/D torque safety. ideaData.dfmDfa: Fewer parts in the crowded bell-housing (resolver stator, screws, cable clips, connector); no resolver-to-rotor angle offset to calibrate and no connector to mis-seat — a recurring P2 assembly issue removed.

title: Sintered ferrite interpole magnets replace NdFeB between the claws of the BSG rotor
description: [MHEV] NdFeB 0.10-0.16 kg × €65-75/kg (€6.5-12) replaced by ~0.25-0.35 kg ferrite × €3-4/kg (€0.8-1.4); no NiCuNi coating; removes rare-earth price exposure. Baseline: high-output claw-pole machines add permanent magnets between adjacent claws (interpole magnets) to cut claw-to-claw leakage flux and lift torque density — a claw-pole construction combining permanent magnets and electrical excitation is patent-protected by Valeo. Where NdFeB is used, a 16-pole rotor carries 16 small blocks, ~0.10-0.16 kg total of N38SH-class material retained by a stainless or PA cage. Proposal: replace with sintered strontium ferrite (Y30BH / SrFe12O19, Br ≈ 0.38-0.40 T vs ~1.25 T) in a deeper block that fills the trapezoidal interpole gap more completely. Because the interpole magnet's job is leakage suppression (counter-MMF across the gap) rather than main flux, a ferrite block of ~2× the volume recovers roughly 60-75% of the NdFeB benefit; the remaining 3-5% torque deficit is recovered with 5-8% more field current (field copper loss rises ~10-15 W, within the field driver rating). Ferrite's positive Hc temperature coefficient means it resists demagnetisation better when hot but worse at −40 °C: check at cold-crank with full field and maximum armature reaction. Ferrite is 5-6× less dense in cost per kg (~€3-4/kg vs €65-75/kg).

title: Diesel I6: BSG warm restarts let pinion cranking motor revert to standard duty
description: [MHEV] Standard-duty starter is €12-18 cheaper than a stop-start starter; ring gear induction-hardening scope and tooth chamfer finishing reduced (€2-3). No new hardware. Baseline: an engine with automatic stop-start normally specifies an enhanced-duty 12 V cranking motor (rated ~250,000-400,000 engagements: reinforced pinion and freewheel, soft-mesh or permanently engaged mechanism, long-life brushes and needle bearings) and a reinforced flexplate tooth rim in C55 with full-flank induction hardening to 50-55 HRC. On the MHEV diesel I6 the pinion motor stays for cold starts (diesel compression and −30 °C friction exceed belt traction), but every warm restart is done by the 48 V belt machine — the BMW split, where the conventional 12 V unit only handles the first cold start of the day. Engagement count therefore falls to ~1-3 per day, roughly 15,000-30,000 over vehicle life, an order of magnitude below the stop-start rating. Proposal: specify the standard-duty (non-stop-start) 2.2-2.7 kW pre-engaged motor already produced in high volume for conventional engines, with standard brushes and sleeve bearings, and a C45 tooth rim with induction hardening limited to the engagement chamfers. Software logs engagements and, if the 48 V machine is unavailable, disables automatic engine-stop so the 12 V motor never accumulates stop-start duty.

title: UV-plus-heat roll-dip impregnation of 48 V stators replaces oven trickle impregnation
description: [MHEV] Cycle 60-100 min (batch oven) → 5-8 min one-piece flow: oven energy and floor space removed; resin use down ~20-30% (no drip and trickle loss); WIP inventory and handling reduced. Baseline: 48 V BSG and P2 stators are commonly trickle-impregnated with an unsaturated-polyester-imide or epoxy resin (rotate, preheat to ~120 °C, trickle 2-4 min, gel, then oven cure 40-90 min at 150-170 °C), the same process used for 400-800 V traction stators. At 48 V the insulation system has no partial-discharge duty: peak phase-to-phase voltage is <70 V, far below the ~400-500 V PDIV of a single grade-2 enamel layer, so the resin's only jobs are mechanical fixing of conductors against vibration, heat-conduction to the core and protection against contamination. Proposal: roll-dip impregnation — the stator rotates with its end-windings dipped in a dual-cure (UV + thermal) acrylate-epoxy resin bath for 30-60 s, end-windings are UV-gelled in 20-40 s, and slot resin is cured by resistive (current) heating of the winding for 3-5 min at ~160 °C instead of a batch oven. Resin consumption falls because there is no trickle overspray and drip-off, and the line becomes one-piece-flow. Applicable to both the BSG (claw-pole) stator and the P2 stator, since both are 48 V.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Replaces a trickle machine + continuous oven (~€2-3M, 40-60 m²) with a roll-dip + UV + current-heating cell (~€1-1.5M, 15-20 m²). Energy per stator drops ~60-70%. VOC emissions reduced with low-styrene/acrylate resin.

title: BSG bolted straight to cast-in block bosses; separate aluminium mounting bracket deleted
timeToImplement: 18-30 months (tied to a block casting update)
description: [MHEV] Deletes the bracket casting and machining (€8-12) and 3-4 bolts (€1); added block boss machining (~€1.5-2.5) and a one-off block/cover tool insert change. Baseline: when a 48 V machine replaces the alternator on an existing engine (the SEG/JLR "in place of the alternator" approach), the heavier, higher-torque machine is usually carried by a separate die-cast EN AC-46000 bracket (~1.2-1.8 kg) bolted to the block with 3-4 M10 bolts, with the BSG bolted to the bracket by 2-3 more. The bracket exists to adapt an old alternator pattern and to add stiffness for belt hub loads of 2.5-3.5 kN during cranking. Proposal: at the next block casting update, cast two stiff mounting bosses (with ribbing) into the block/front cover and bolt the BSG's housing ears directly — three M10 10.9 bolts with machined faces and one dowel for belt-plane alignment (±0.3 mm pulley-plane tolerance). Stiffness check: bracket compliance is a main contributor to BSG mount resonance; a block-integrated mount typically pushes the first mode from ~400-500 Hz to >700 Hz, clear of the 3rd-order firing excitation at max speed (~300 Hz at 6,000 rpm) and its low harmonics. Belt-plane alignment improves because one interface is removed from the tolerance stack.

title: Edgewise helical-wound M400-50A strip core replaces stamped M330-35A rings in BSG stator
description: [MHEV] Gross steel per stator falls from ~3.0 kg to ~1.7 kg; grade price drops ~€0.2-0.3/kg; punching strokes halve with 0.5 mm strip. Combined ≈ €3-4 per stator. Baseline: a premium 48 V belt machine stator core is often stamped as full annular laminations from 0.35 mm M330-35A non-oriented steel and welded/cleated into a stack (~1.3-1.6 kg finished). The ring blank leaves the bore and the outer web as scrap, so material utilisation is ~40-50%. Proposal: an edgewise helically wound core — a straight strip with the teeth punched in a progressive die is bent edgewise into a helix on a mandrel, compressed and welded axially, the process used for automotive alternator stators. Utilisation rises to ~85-90%. Grade: move to 0.50 mm M400-50A. Justification: the claw-pole BSG runs at fundamental frequency f = p × n/60 = 8 × 18,000/60 = 2.4 kHz only at maximum speed and spends most of its life at 300-1,200 Hz; iron loss at 1.0 T/400 Hz rises from ~9-10 W/kg (M330-35A) to ~14-16 W/kg (M400-50A), about 25-40 W extra at mid-speed — ~0.5-1 percentage point of efficiency on a 6 kW generating point, acceptable for a belt machine whose efficiency is dominated by copper and claw-pole leakage. Thicker strip halves the number of laminations (faster punching) and is cheaper per kg.

title: Electrostatic epoxy powder-coated slots replace NMN slot liners in 48 V stators
description: [MHEV] Liner material (€1.0-1.5) and insertion (€0.6-1.0) replaced by powder and coating (€0.6-0.9); slot-fill gain worth ~€0.3-0.6 in copper/stack. Bonding by powder also removes stack welding or cleats on some designs. Baseline: many 48 V BSG and P2 stators carry over traction-motor slot insulation: a 0.25-0.30 mm NMN (aramid paper/PET film/aramid paper) or DMD laminate liner, cut, creased, cuffed at both ends and inserted into each slot (36-72 slots) before winding. At 48 V the dielectric duty is trivial (<70 V peak, no partial discharge), so the liner is really there to protect enamel from lamination burrs and to give a creepage barrier at the core ends. Proposal: fluidised-bed or electrostatic epoxy powder coating of the stator core (e.g. a class-F/H epoxy powder at 0.15-0.20 mm in the slots, cured 10-15 min at 180-200 °C), which simultaneously covers burrs, insulates slot walls and the core end faces, and bonds the lamination stack. This is a long-established insulation method for small low-voltage motors and armatures. The thinner wall (0.15-0.20 vs 0.25-0.30 mm) frees ~3-5% slot area, which can be given to copper (lower resistance) or used to shorten the stack. Remove liner cutting/insertion stations; masking on bore and OD (air-gap and housing fits) by removable plugs or post-grinding the bore.

title: HPDC EN AC-46000 BSG housing with FSW-sealed jacket replaces sand-cored T6 gravity casting
description: [MHEV] No sand core (€1.5-2.5), no T6 (€0.4-0.6/kg ≈ €1), 3-4× faster casting cycle (€2-3), cheaper secondary alloy (€0.5-0.8); minus FSW cover (€1.5-2.0 incl. cover). Baseline: water-cooled 48 V belt machines (the Audi Q7/Q8 BAS is water-cooled) need a closed annular coolant passage around the stator. A common route is gravity or low-pressure die casting in EN AC-42100 (AlSi7Mg0.3) with a resin-bonded sand core forming the passage, then decoring, T6 heat treatment (solution ~540 °C + ageing ~160 °C, 8-10 h total) and machining; ~4-6 min per cavity. Proposal: vacuum high-pressure die cast the BSG housing in secondary EN AC-46000 (AlSi9Cu3(Fe)) with an open-deck groove formed by die slides and open toward the pulley-end face, then close the groove with a stamped EN AW-6063 ring joined by friction-stir welding (FSW, ~60-80 s, 2-3 mm penetration). Shot cycle is ~70-90 s for a 2-2.5 kg part; there is no sand core and no T6 (as-cast use avoids blistering trapped gas). As-cast yield of ~140-160 MPa covers belt hub loads of ~3-3.5 kN through the bearing seat. Conductivity drops from ~150 to ~110 W/m·K, negligible against the coolant film resistance. The idea is about a small belt-machine shell, made by the million in alternator-sized cells.

title: BSG pulley flow-formed from S420MC disc replaces pulley turned from C45 bar

Net about €1.5-2.5 per pulley. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Bought steel per pulley falls from ~0.6 kg bar (€1.1-1.4/kg) to ~0.38 kg plate (€0.9-1.0/kg); turning time 60-90 s → finish turn 10-15 s; lower inertia slightly reduces belt peak forces. Net about €1.5-2.5 per pulley.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Flow-forming cell (~€0.8-1.2M) with 25-35 s cycle replaces two CNC turning cells; chip handling and coolant use drop sharply. Pulley supplier capacity is commodity (same machines as crank and coolant-pump pulleys).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Interface to the BSG shaft unchanged (same bore, nut and torque spec), so the machine design carries over. Lighter pulley eases handling at the machine end-of-line balancing station; rib profile verified by 100% laser gauging.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — small but certain per-part saving
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Steel 0.6 kg × €1.25/kg = €0.75 → 0.38 kg × €0.95/kg = €0.36 (−€0.39); turning 60-90 s × €1.2/min = €1.2-1.8 → flow-form + finish 35-50 s × €1.0/min ≈ €0.6-0.8 (−€0.6-1.0); coating on 25% less area −€0.1-0.2; tooling/capex amortisation −€0.0 to +€0.1; rounded with scrap/handling €0.4-0.9 → €1.5-2.5 per vehicle × 50,000 = €0.075M-0.125M.

ideaData.riskNotes: Rib-tip fatigue and hub cracking under torque reversal and nut clamp must be shown by rotating-bending and torsional fatigue rigs at 1.5x peak torque; rib profile accuracy (ISO 9981 / SAE J1459 poly-V) affects belt noise — validate squeal and belt wear on engine rig. title: Narrower 6PK aramid-cord EPDM belt replaces 8PK polyester belt on the BSG drive
description: [MHEV] Belt cost roughly neutral (aramid premium offset by 25% less width) but 5-7 pulleys each narrower (€0.3-0.6 each), lower static tension cuts tensioner spring and bearing size; longer belt life removes a scheduled replacement in some markets. Baseline: some 48 V belt drives keep a wide 8PK EPDM belt with polyester (PET) tensile cord and a higher static tension (~600-800 N per span) to stop slip under BSG cranking and regen torque reversals. PET cord stretches and creeps over life, so the tensioner must cover a large take-up and the static tension starts high. Proposal: 6PK EPDM belt with aramid tensile cord, as used by Toyota on the Land Cruiser Hybrid 48V (high-strength, aramid-reinforced belt with dual-arm tensioner). Aramid modulus is ~4-5× PET, so elongation under peak torque and long-term creep are much lower: the dual-arm tensioner holds a near-constant tension with a smaller stroke, and the allowed tight-side force per rib can rise. Per-rib capacity: a 6PK aramid belt at ~450-500 N/rib allowable tight-side force (≈2,800 N) matches a ~66 Nm machine at a 58 mm pulley, while an 8PK PET belt at ~350 N/rib reaches the same force only with two more ribs. Two fewer ribs narrow every pulley in the drive (crank damper/pulley, BSG pulley, idlers, tensioner pulleys, coolant pump) by ~7 mm — less material, shorter front-end stack-up and a smaller damper hub.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Pulley narrowing 6 × €0.3-0.6 = €1.8-3.6; tensioner spring/bearing downsizing €0.8-1.2; belt delta €0-0.2 saving (aramid premium offset by 25% less width) → €2.6-5.0, i.e. €2.5-5 per vehicle × 50,000 = €0.125M-0.25M.

title: Diamond friction shim in crank pulley joint carries BSG reversing torque, key deleted
description: [MHEV] Removes keyway milling on the crank nose and broaching on the hub (€2-3), the key (€0.2), and avoids an upsized bolt and harder hub material (€1-2); adds a shim (~€0.6-1.0). Baseline: a BSG reverses torque through the crank pulley/torsional-vibration-damper joint — driving the crank at up to ~180 Nm during cranking and boost, braking it during regen — on top of the firing-order torsional oscillation. Engine programmes typically respond by upgrading the central-bolt joint: adding a Woodruff key or a broached/spline hub, a larger M16-M18 10.9/12.9 bolt or a higher clamp load, because a purely frictional joint at μ ≈ 0.12-0.15 risks micro-slip, fretting and loss of timing reference. Proposal: keep a plain cylindrical hub and standard central bolt but insert a diamond friction shim (nickel-plated steel shim with embedded diamond particles, the product formerly sold as ESK EKagrip, now 3M Friction Shims) between the damper hub and the crank sprocket/nose shoulder. 3M states μ can exceed 0.6 and joints transmit up to 4× higher torque without redesign, and lists central-bolt crankshaft and camshaft joints as typical applications. Joint capacity: T = μ × F_clamp × r_eff × n_interfaces; with F = 90 kN, r_eff = 22 mm, μ rising from 0.14 to 0.5 (conservative) the slip torque goes from ~280 Nm to ~990 Nm on one interface — ample margin over BSG peak plus torsional amplitude. title: Net-shape warm-forged C10C claw-pole halves skip the BSG rotor OD turning operation
description: [MHEV] Billet weight reduced ~8-12% (less scale/allowance); claw OD and chamfer turning deleted (2-3 min machine time per pair); tool wear and chips reduced. Sizing press stroke adds a small cost. Baseline: claw-pole rotor halves for a 48 V belt machine (16-pole, ~95-105 mm OD) are commonly hot forged (~1,150-1,250 °C) from low-carbon steel billets, then shot-blasted, and machined on bore, faces, claw OD and claw chamfers to hold the air gap (typically 0.30-0.40 mm) and balance — several minutes of turning per pair, with scale loss of ~2-3% and machining allowance ~1-1.5 mm on the claw OD. Proposal: warm forging at ~750-900 °C from C10C (1.0214) or equivalent cold-heading steel, followed by a cold coining/sizing stroke on the claw fingers, delivering the claw outer diameter and chamfers net-shape (IT9-IT10, ±0.05 mm after sizing). Only the bore, the pole-core contact faces and a final light skim of the assembled rotor OD (or no skim, if the air gap allows ±0.05 mm) remain. Warm forging cuts scale and allowance, keeps fine grain for good magnetic permeability (low carbon, no hardening) and needs a magnetic anneal only if cold work in the claw degrades permeability beyond spec (check B-H at 5,000 A/m). The rotor with field coil, interpole magnets and slip ring is then assembled as today.

title: Central 48 V bus clamp lets inverter and DC-DC use 80 V MOSFETs
description: [MHEV] Silicon area per switch falls ~35% at equal loss, so 6 fewer MOSFETs in the inverter and ~4 fewer in the DC-DC (and fewer in e-ARB/e-compressor drives); smaller snubbers. The 48 V battery's MOSFET disconnect is combined with a central active clamp (a 58 V-standoff TVS array plus an inverter-commanded active short circuit on the BiSG, which is the only source able to generate a load-dump) so that the vehicle 48 V node is guaranteed ≤60 V; the OEM component specification for the inverter and DC-DC is then written to 60 V long-term / 64 V transient instead of 70 V. Proposal: move the overvoltage protection to one place. The 48 V battery's MOSFET disconnect is combined with a central active clamp (a 58 V-standoff TVS array plus an inverter-commanded active short circuit on the BiSG, which is the only source able to generate a load-dump) so that the vehicle 48 V node is guaranteed ≤60 V; the OEM component specification for the inverter and DC-DC is then written to 60 V long-term / 64 V transient instead of 70 V. The BiSG inverter goes from 4 to 3 devices per switch (24 → 18) and the DC-DC from 2 to 1-2 per switch at equal conduction loss. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Silicon area per switch falls ~35% at equal loss, so 6 fewer MOSFETs in the inverter and ~4 fewer in the DC-DC (and fewer in e-ARB/e-compressor drives); smaller snubbers. The one central clamp costs less than the per-unit margin it removes.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: No new processes; fewer SMT placements (~10-14) and smaller power-stage area (~15%); the battery gains one TVS array assembly. Re-validation of every 48 V component against the revised OEM specification is the main effort.

title: BiSG inverter on engine HT coolant via top-side-cooled MOSFETs deletes LT branch
description: [MHEV] Removes the LT-branch auxiliary pump, switching valve, ~2.5 m hose and clips, and one LT radiator section share; the HT tap uses existing engine coolant pressure. Engine-control software takes over the pump logic the inverter used to run. Baseline: the liquid-cooled 48 V BiSG inverter (and DC-DC) sits on the low-temperature (LT, ≤65 °C) loop, which on the I6 MHEV means a dedicated branch: an electric 12 V auxiliary pump (~15-20 W), a thermostatic or switching valve, ~2.5 m of hose with 6 clips and a cross-feed to the LT radiator. Proposal: cool the inverter from the engine high-temperature circuit (≤105-110 °C coolant) tapped at the cylinder-head outlet next to the BiSG mount, deleting the LT branch, valve and pump. This is enabled by top-side-cooled 100 V MOSFETs (TOLT): with RthJC about 50% lower than TOLL, a 1.5 mΩ device dissipating 25 W at peak boost sees ΔT(junction-coolant) of ~45-55 K through RthJC + insulating TIM + cold plate, so Tj stays ≤165 °C at 110 °C coolant — within the 175 °C rating with margin. Gate driver and MCU sit on the board area away from the cold plate with ≤125 °C component rating (AEC-Q100 Grade 1). Boost torque is derated above 108 °C coolant (rare, at hot towing at 3,500 kg). Benchmarks: Audi's 48 V BAS is water-cooled and controls its own coolant pump; Infineon's TOLT 100 V MOSFET targets 48 V starter generators up to 30 kW.

title: One 48 V half-bridge power cell reused in BiSG, e-ARB, e-compressor and fan drives
description: [MHEV] Directed-buy volume on one or two MOSFET part numbers (typically 8-12% lower price than five separate supplier buys), one gate-driver family, and shared qualification/characterisation spend amortised over all drives; fewer obsolescence and second-source management cases. Baseline: the luxury SUV MHEV runs five or more 48 V motor drives from different suppliers — BiSG inverter (~400 A phase), two e-ARB actuators (~80-120 A), the 48 V electric climate compressor, the 850 W engine fan and on some trims a 48 V electric booster — each with its own MOSFET part number (3-4 different 80/100 V devices), gate driver, shunt and layout, each separately qualified. Proposal: specify one 48 V 'power cell' — a half-bridge sub-layout of 100 V TOLT MOSFETs (1.5-1.9 mΩ class, one part number per current class), one three-phase gate-driver family and one low-side shunt/current-sense design — that every 48 V drive supplier must use, scaling by paralleling 1, 2 or 3 devices per switch. title: 48/12 V DC-DC sized to measured 12 V load with trim-based phase population
description: [MHEV] Base trims (~70% of mix) lose 2 phases and mid/top trims 1: fewer MOSFETs, inductors, CSAs, gate-driver channels and smaller output capacitors; the same PCB, housing and software serve all variants so no new tooling. Baseline: one 3.0-3.5 kW bidirectional 48/12 V DC-DC (5 interleaved phases, 10 × 100 V MOSFETs, 5 inductors) fitted to every trim, sized for the worst-case 12 V load of the top trim with every heater and the sum of fuse ratings. Since heated glazing, seat heating and the engine fan have moved to 48 V on the luxury SUV, the measured 12 V continuous demand in fleet data is typically 1.2-1.8 kW, with peaks covered by the 12 V battery. Proposal: one PCB with five phase footprints, populated with 3 phases (2.0-2.2 kW) on base/mid trims and 4 phases (2.8 kW) on top trims with rear-seat entertainment and heavy 12 V content; the 12 V AGM battery buffers peaks of ≤10 s; a load-management priority list sheds comfort loads before the DC-DC current limit. title: Top-side-cooled TOLT power stage on FR4 deletes aluminium IMS and board-to-board pins
description: [MHEV] IMS substrate and its screw set deleted, 40 press-fit pins and stand-offs deleted, 6 fewer MOSFETs; one board instead of two means one SMT/AOI/ICT flow. The added insulating pad is cheaper than the IMS it replaces. Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter power stage is 24 bottom-cooled 100 V MOSFETs (D2PAK-7/TOLL, 4 per switch) reflowed on a 1.5 mm aluminium insulated-metal substrate (single 140 µm Cu layer, 2.2 W/mK dielectric) screwed to the cold plate, plus a separate 6-layer FR4 gate-drive/control board joined by ~40 press-fit pins and stand-offs, with phase and DC busbars soldered/screwed to the IMS. Proposal: one 6-layer FR4 (IPC-4101/126, Tg 170, 2 × 105 µm outer, 2 × 70 µm inner) carrying 18 TOLT MOSFETs (3 per switch, 1.5 mΩ class), gate drivers and MCU; the TOLT exposes the drain on top, so the board is flipped and the MOSFET tops press onto the cold plate through a 0.2 mm electrically insulating gap pad (≥3 W/mK, ≥4 kV breakdown) — needed because the half-bridges' drains sit at different potentials. Heat no longer crosses the PCB, so the board need not be IMS. Physics: Infineon states TOLT achieves ~50% better RthJC and ~20% better RthJA than TOLL, allowing >20% more power and less board cooling effort — enough to cut from 4 to 3 devices per switch at equal Tj (I²R per device rises by (4/3)² = 1.78 but the thermal path improves ~2×). Benchmark: Infineon's IAUS300N10S

title: Inductor-DCR current sensing in the 48/12 V DC-DC deletes per-phase shunts
description: [MHEV] Removes 4-5 phase shunts and 3-4 discrete current-sense amplifiers (the multiphase controller's differential inputs take the RC signal); 4-7 W less loss lowers cold-plate/heat-sink demand and raises efficiency, helping the 12 V energy balance. Baseline: a 4-5 phase interleaved 48/12 V DC-DC measures each phase current with a 0.5 mΩ 4-terminal metal-strip shunt (2512/3920 size) in the 12 V output path plus one current-sense amplifier per phase, and a further shunt in the 48 V input for power limiting. At 40-55 A per phase each shunt dissipates 0.8-1.5 W, i.e. 4-7 W total — ~0.2 percentage points of efficiency at 3 kW. Proposal: sense each phase across the power inductor's own winding resistance (DCR ≈ 0.4-0.6 mΩ) with a matched RC network (R·C = L/DCR) feeding the controller's differential inputs, temperature-compensated by an NTC mounted on the inductor cluster; keep one precision 0.25 mΩ shunt on the total 12 V output for absolute accuracy and auto-calibrate each phase's DCR against it at every power-up and periodically in operation. Per-phase balancing only needs ±5% matching, the absolute ±1-2% comes from the single output shunt. Benchmark context: published four- and five-phase interleaved 48/12 V converters depend on per-phase current control for interleaving and ripple cancellation — this keeps that control while removing the dissipative per-phase sensors.

title: Air-cooled finned DC-DC in the dry rear bay replaces liquid-cooled underbonnet unit
description: [MHEV] Deletes the coolant spigots, O-ring groove machining, leak test, two hoses and quick connectors and the coolant routing; shortens the heavy 48 V cable run; the fan and fins cost less than the cooling hardware removed. Baseline: the 3 kW 48/12 V DC-DC is liquid-cooled, mounted underbonnet or under the floor on the LT coolant loop: a cold-plate HPDC EN AC-46000 housing with machined O-ring grooves and two spigots, two hoses with quick connectors, ~1.8 m of extra coolant routing, a leak test and a bracket. Proposal: move the converter next to the 48 V battery in the rear luggage-floor dry zone (where the 12 V battery and 48 V battery already sit on many luxury SUVs) and cool it by air: a finned HPDC EN AC-46000 housing (fin height 25 mm, pitch 6 mm, effective area ~0.3 m²) with natural convection plus a 48 V 60 mm fan run only above 1.5 kW. At 2.2-2.8 kW and 96.5-97% efficiency the loss is 70-95 W; at h ≈ 15-20 W/m²K with the fan, ΔT(fin-air) ≈ 15-20 K, so 55 °C cabin-side ambient keeps the MOSFETs well inside their rating. The 48 V input cable is now ~0.4 m instead of ~4 m, while the 12 V output feeds the rear 12 V battery/fuse box directly. Benchmarks: commercial 48 V DC-DC converters list air cooling, to reduce integration cost, as a core feature, and a demonstrated 48/12 V converter delivered 97% at 2.4 kW in buck mode, 'promising where water cooling must be avoided'.

title: Hybrid polymer 63 V capacitor bank replaces metallised-film DC-link block in BiSG inverter
description: [MHEV] Catalogue SMT parts from 3-4 competing makers replace a custom single-source film block with busbars and potting; the DC-link busbar lamination disappears because the caps sit on the PCB copper; assembly moves into the SMT reflow. Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter uses a custom metallised-polypropylene film DC-link block (~600-800 µF, 75-100 V, ~150 A rms ripple) with integrated laminated copper busbars, potted in a PPS case and screwed or welded to the power stage — a single-source custom part at €18-25. Proposal: a distributed bank of 30-32 surface-mount conductive-polymer hybrid aluminium electrolytic capacitors (63 V, 150 µF, ~5.0-5.2 A rms each at 100 kHz/125 °C, Φ10 × 16.5 mm) placed directly beside each half-bridge on the power PCB, plus 12-18 × 100 V X7R 1210 MLCCs at each switch pair for the high-frequency loop. Totals: ~4.5-4.8 mF and ~155 A rms ripple capability — more capacitance than the film block, which also damps belt-induced bus resonance. Hybrid caps combine liquid electrolyte with conductive polymer for low ESR and high ripple, so the classic liquid-electrolytic ripple limit no longer forces a film solution at 48 V. Benchmarks: Panasonic proposes a 63 V 180 µF hybrid configuration for 48 V systems; 63 V 150 µF hybrid parts are rated ~5.0-5.2 A rms in 10 × 16.5 mm and 12.5 × 13.5 mm cases; Nichicon has extended high-ripple hybrid series to 63 V.

ideaData.title: Hybrid polymer 63 V capacitor bank replaces metallised-film DC-link block in BiSG inverter
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter uses a custom metallised-polypropylene film DC-link block (~600-800 µF, 75-100 V, ~150 A rms ripple) with integrated laminated copper busbars, potted in a PPS case and screwed or welded to the power stage — a single-source custom part at €18-25. Proposal: a distributed bank of 30-32 surface-mount conductive-polymer hybrid aluminium electrolytic capacitors (63 V, 150 µF, ~5.0-5.2 A rms each at 100 kHz/125 °C, Φ10 × 16.5 mm) placed directly beside each half-bridge on the power PCB, plus 12-18 × 100 V X7R 1210 MLCCs at each switch pair for the high-frequency loop. Totals: ~4.5-4.8 mF and ~155 A rms ripple capability — more capacitance than the film block, which also damps belt-induced bus resonance. Hybrid caps combine liquid electrolyte with conductive polymer for low ESR and high ripple, so the classic liquid-electrolytic ripple limit no longer forces a film solution at 48 V. Benchmarks: Panasonic proposes a 63 V 180 µF hybrid configuration for 48 V systems; 63 V 150 µF hybrid parts are rated ~5.0-5.2 A rms in 10 × 16.5 mm and 12.5 × 13.5 mm cases; Nichicon has extended high-ripple hybrid series to 63 V.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Catalogue SMT parts from 3-4 competing makers replace a custom single-source film block with busbars and potting; the DC-link busbar lamination disappears because the caps sit on the PCB copper; assembly moves into the SMT reflow.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Film block screwing/welding station and its potting removed (~45 s); 30 extra SMT placements (~6 s); reflow profile must respect the hybrid caps' peak (check 245-260 °C rating); no new capex.
ideaData.dfmDfa: One fewer custom part, one fewer bolted/welded joint set; distributed caps reduce loop inductance so snubbers can be smaller; catalogue parts ease second sourcing.

Net €6-€10 per vehicle × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €300K-€500K/yr. Piece costs are engineering estimates at this volume, not supplier quotes.

title: Two-phase coupled-inductor pairs halve magnetics count in silicon 48/12 V DC-DC
description: [MHEV] Two cores and two winding sets replace four; less core and copper mass for equal ripple; smaller output capacitor bank; half the inductor placements and solder/weld terminations. Baseline: the silicon-MOSFET 48/12 V DC-DC (4 phases at 100-150 kHz) uses four discrete 4.7-6.8 µH power inductors (powder toroid or ferrite with flat-wire winding, ~120-180 g each), each sized for its own peak current plus ripple. Proposal: two inversely coupled two-phase inductors — each a single EE/EI ferrite-and-gap or powder core carrying two windings with coupling k ≈ −0.7 — for the same 4 phases, keeping silicon 100 V MOSFETs (this is NOT the GaN route already in the library). In inverse coupling the DC fluxes of the two phases cancel in the shared core leg, so the core only has to carry the ripple flux plus leakage; the steady-state phase ripple falls and its frequency doubles in the shared output, while the transient (leakage) inductance stays low for fast load response. Net: two magnetic components instead of four, ~35-45% less core volume and copper for the same ripple, and output capacitance can drop ~25%. Benchmark: a published four-phase bidirectional 48/12 V converter with coupled inductors in interleaving mode cut peak-to-peak current ripple to 8 A, at double the switching frequency.

title: FeSiAl powder core replaces High-Flux FeNi50 core in DC-DC phase inductors
description: [MHEV] Nickel-free FeSiAl alloy powder replaces 50% Ni alloy powder, removing nickel price exposure: core price falls ~40-55% per piece; the small extra copper turn offsets only part of it. Baseline: 48/12 V DC-DC phase inductors (4.7 µH, 45-55 A DC per phase, 100-150 kHz) wound on High-Flux (Fe-50%Ni alloy powder, µ=60) toroids, chosen for their ~1.5 T saturation and soft DC-bias roll-off; nickel content makes them the most expensive powder-core family after MPP. Proposal: FeSiAl (Sendust, 85% Fe / 9% Si / 6% Al, µ=60) toroids of the same OD class, with turns increased ~10-15% (≈ +1 turn on 8-9) and flat-wire Cu-ETP (CW004A) re-sized to hold DCR, to recover inductance under DC bias since Sendust saturates near 1 T. Sendust's lower core loss at 100-150 kHz than High-Flux partly offsets the extra copper loss, and its near-zero magnetostriction cuts audible whine at light-load burst mode. A sourced cost ranking puts Sendust as 'low' relative cost, ferrite lowest and molybdenum-permalloy higher; Sendust gives good DC bias and low magnetostriction in the 20-500 kHz range and is recommended alongside iron powder for automotive 48 V converters with large DC bias. Ferrite is not chosen because its 0.3-0.5 T saturation and steep fall-off above 100 °C would force gapped EE cores with fringing loss in the 12 V high-current path.

title: 210 µm heavy-copper inner layers replace stamped Cu-ETP 12 V output busbar in DC-DC
description: [MHEV] Deletes the stamped busbar, its tin plating, 6 screws, the screw station and the busbar-to-stud joint; the heavy-copper PCB price premium (~€1.6-1.8 on this board size) is less than the busbar assembly cost. Baseline: the 48/12 V DC-DC collects the four phase outputs (up to 250 A) on a stamped CW004A (Cu-ETP) 2 × 12 mm tin-plated busbar screwed to PCB pads with 6 × M4 screws and joined to the 12 V M8 output stud, because the 6-layer FR4 power board (2 × 70 µm outer, 4 × 35 µm inner) cannot carry the current. Proposal: a 6-layer FR4 IPC-4101/126 (Tg 170) with two internal 210 µm (6 oz) copper planes dedicated to the 12 V output and ground return, outer layers 105 µm. Two 210 µm planes 60 mm wide give 25 mm² cross-section per polarity — comparable to the stamped bar's 24 mm² — and the current spreads in parallel through stitched vias (~120 × 0.5 mm plated vias per transition). The 12 V output stud is press-fitted into the board through a compliant-pin base. Physics: at 250 A and ~0.07 mΩ plane resistance the plane loses ~4.5 W, conducted directly into the cold-plate-mounted board area — equivalent to the busbar's loss. Benchmark context: top-side-cooled MOSFET packages such as TOLT reduce the cooling effort on the board, which is what frees the inner layers to be used as conductors rather than heat spreaders.

title: Cold-headed CuZn37 48 V B+ terminal stud replaces turned leaded-brass CuZn39Pb3 stud
description: [MHEV] Cold heading replaces CNC turning (cycle cost falls ~80%) and scrap/swarf drops from ~45% to ~5% of input brass; lead-free alloy avoids future ELV exemption-expiry redesign. Baseline: the 48 V B+ (and 12 V output) terminals on the BiSG inverter and DC-DC are M8 studs turned from CuZn39Pb3 (CW614N) free-cutting brass bar on CNC sliding-head lathes (~35-45 s cycle, ~55% material yield), knurled, then tin-plated, and insert-moulded or pressed into the housing; at 2-3 studs per vehicle on the 48 V units. Proposal: cold-headed and thread-rolled CuZn37 (CW508L) studs — a lead-free brass with good cold-forming ductility — formed in a 3-station header (~150-200 parts/min) with a forged hex/knurl collar, thread rolled (stronger thread root than cut), then tin plated. Material yield rises to ~95%, and the part avoids reliance on the ELV Annex II lead-in-copper-alloy exemption. CuZn37 conductivity (~15 MS/m) is close to CuZn39Pb3 (~15 MS/m), so terminal temperature rise at the 250-400 A of a 48 V B+ joint is unchanged; the current flows mainly through the ring lug clamped face anyway. Benchmark context: the 48 V B+ terminal carries the full machine current — Audi's 48 V BAS delivers up to 12 kW, i.e. 250 A-class at 48 V.

title: Deep-drawn EN AW-5754 cover replaces machined HPDC EN AC-46000 cover on DC-DC
description: [MHEV] Deletes a die-cast part with its die, trimming, machining of flange and bosses, and FIPG dispensing; a progressive/transfer draw part costs ~40% of the machined casting and weighs a third. Baseline: the 48/12 V DC-DC enclosure is two HPDC EN AC-46000 (AlSi9Cu3(Fe)) castings — the cold-plate base and a 2.5-3.0 mm wall cover (~420 g) with a machined sealing flange, 8 machined M5 bosses and an FIPG silicone bead, chosen historically for EMC shielding and stiffness. Proposal: replace the cover with a deep-drawn EN AW-5754-H111 sheet (1.2 mm), draw depth ~30 mm with embossed stiffening ribs and a flat flange, sealed by a moulded EPDM or LSR profile gasket captured in the base casting's groove and fastened with 8 thread-forming screws into cored holes in the base. Mass ~150 g (−65%). Shielding: 1.2 mm aluminium gives >60 dB absorption loss above 1 MHz (skin depth of Al at 1 MHz ≈ 0.08 mm), so CISPR 25 radiated performance is unchanged provided the flange has metal-to-metal contact at ≤30 mm screw pitch or a conductive gasket section. Stiffness: drawn ribs raise the first panel mode above 800 Hz, clear of ISO 16750-3 random-vibration peaks. Benchmark context: commercial 48 V DC-DC converters are offered as air-cooled units designed to reduce integration cost (Eaton) — the cover no longer needs to be a thermal casting, which is what makes sheet viable.

title: One 16-way sealed hybrid connector replaces three LV connectors on the 48 V inverter
description: [MHEV] Two header bodies, two seals, two CPAs, two harness-side housings and two machined connector openings in the housing are deleted; one hybrid header costs less than three separate ones and the harness loses two breakouts. Baseline: the 48 V BiSG inverter carries three low-voltage connector interfaces on the housing — a 2-way 12 V supply/KL15 wake connector (2.8 mm terminals), a 6-way CAN-FD + private-CAN connector (0.64 mm), and a 4-way connector for the coolant pump/temperature sensor (or machine temperature/position sensor) — each a sealed header with its own PBT-GF30 shroud, interface seal, CPA and harness-side mating part. Proposal: one 16-way sealed hybrid header in PBT-GF30 with 2 × 2.8 mm and 14 × 0.64 mm cavities (CuSn6 tin-plated terminals for signal, CuNiSi for the 2.8 mm power pins), one interface seal, one CPA and one secondary lock. The private-CAN pair, sensor lines and 12 V supply share one harness branch; wake and fail-safe lines keep dedicated pins. Benchmark: Audi's 48 V generator is linked to the engine ECU on its own CAN bus and controls its own coolant pump — i.e. power, CAN and pump-control lines all terminate at the machine electronics, which is exactly the signal set that can be consolidated into one header.

title: As-cast pin-fin cooling face replaces machined cold-plate face on inverter housing
description: [MHEV] Deletes friction-stir welding of the channel cover (~60 s), CNC fly-cutting of the contact face (~45 s) and the aluminium cover plate; a moulded lid and gasket are cheaper; pin fins add no machining. Baseline: the liquid-cooled 48 V inverter/DC-DC housing is HPDC EN AC-46000 with a separate cooling channel closed by a friction-stir-welded or screwed EN AW-6063 cover, and the power-stage contact face is CNC fly-cut to 0.05 mm flatness and Ra 1.6 because the bottom-cooled MOSFETs on an IMS need a thin, uniform TIM. Proposal: (a) cast the coolant side as an open pin-fin field (Ø3 mm pins, 6 mm pitch, 12 mm tall, draft 1°) in EN AC-43400 (AlSi10Mg(Fe)), whose better fluidity fills thin pins, closed by a PA66-GF30 or stamped EN AW-5754 lid with a moulded EPDM gasket; (b) leave the electronics contact face as-cast (flatness 0.15-0.2 mm, Ra 3.2-6.3) and absorb the tolerance with a 0.5 mm compliant gap pad, which top-side-cooled TOLT devices tolerate because their RthJC is ~50% lower than TOLL, so the extra pad ΔT (~4-6 K at 25 W/device) is affordable. Pin fins at 6-8 L/min raise h to ~6,000-9,000 W/m²K vs ~3,000 for a plain channel, compensating the thicker pad. Net: friction-stir welding and the CNC face operation disappear. Benchmark: Infineon states TOLT's 50% better RthJC reduces board cooling effort, which is what buys the as-cast tolerance.

title: LV 148 segregation keeps 48 V out of 12 V connectors, sparing ECU hardening
description: [MHEV] Avoided protection upgrade on 10-15 12 V ECUs (higher-voltage clamp, series MOSFET and capacitors at roughly €0.9-€1.5 per ECU) minus the extra conduit, clips and separate inline connectors that physical segregation needs. Baseline: on a luxury-SUV MHEV the 48 V feeds to the starter-generator, e-compressor, active roll actuators, PTC heater and DC-DC are often laid into the same bundles, inline connectors and ECU headers as 12 V circuits. Because a chafed or mis-mated 48 V conductor can then reach any 12 V pin, the conservative answer is to harden every 12 V ECU in those bundles against a 48-58 V fault (60-80 V clamps, 100 V reverse/series MOSFETs, 63 V input capacitors) — 10-15 ECUs on a full-option SUV. Proposal: make segregation a harness rule set instead of a component requirement: (1) 48 V conductors never share a connector housing or inline joint with 12 V except inside dual-voltage ECUs, which carry the 48→12 V short-circuit case themselves (LV 148 E48-21); (2) 48 V wires run in their own conduit branch with a distinct colour/marking and at least one fixing separating them from 12 V bundles; (3) 48 V and 12 V cavities in dual-voltage headers sit on opposite ends with a moulded creepage wall. The 12 V ECUs then keep 40 V-class protection. Physics: a 48-to-12 V short needs two insulation failures in physically separated bundles, rather than one pin misalignment. Ben

Benchmark: in the Audi 48 V system the only 48 V wires run from the belt alternator-starter to the 48 V battery and on to the DC-DC in the luggage compartment, all other systems staying natively 12 V — the confinement principle we formalise for a luxury SUV with more 48 V consumers.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Distinct 48 V colour/marking and keyed 48 V-only housings make mis-mating impossible; fewer ECU hardware variants (no "48 V-hardened" 12 V ECU build); service technicians can identify 48 V branches visually.

title: Hard-wired airbag crash line opens 48 V battery switch, deleting pyrotechnic safety terminal
description: [MHEV] Deletes the pyrotechnic terminal (€12-16), the airbag ECU squib channel and its harness loop (€1.5-2.5) and post-crash replacement cost; adds an isolated hardware crash input and redundant gate path on the BMS (€2.5-3.5). Baseline: MHEVs commonly carry a pyrotechnic battery safety terminal (BST) in the 48 V positive cable, fired by a squib channel of the airbag ECU in a collision; it is single-use, adds a squib loop and connector, and after a minor crash leaves a no-start vehicle needing a part replacement. Proposal: where the 48 V battery already has a solid-state main switch (back-to-back MOSFETs), give the BMS a dedicated hard-wired crash input from the airbag ECU (pulse-coded, plus redundant CAN crash message) that opens the switch through an independent gate-pull-down path that bypasses the BMS microcontroller, with switching in well under 1 ms. The opening is resettable after inspection by diagnostic tool. The battery-side cable stub remains live, so it is kept short (battery in the dry cabin zone) and fully insulated. Physics: 48 V is below the 60 V DC limit of hazardous voltage, so the disconnect is a fire/short-circuit prevention function rather than shock protection — a requirement a properly diagnosed semiconductor switch can satisfy if its fail-short case is covered by a series melting fuse. title: 48 V main cable routed in-cabin above wade line, deleting underbody shields
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Underbody stone-guard shield (€6-8), abrasion sleeve over ~4 m (€4-5), 10-14 sealed underbody clips (€2.5-3.5) deleted; added interior PP channel and one IP67 dash pass-through (€4-6). Baseline: with the 48 V battery under the boot floor and the starter-generator on the engine, the 48 V main cable typically runs ~4.5 m along the underbody or outer sill in a PA6 corrugated conduit, under a moulded stone-guard shield, held by 10-14 sealed underbody clips and entering the body through sealed grommets. On an off-road SUV that cable is submerged at 900 mm wading and exposed to rock strike and abrasion. Proposal: route it inside the body — through one sealed grommet in the boot floor, along the tunnel or inner sill under the carpet in a snap-in PP channel, and out through one IP67 dash pass-through high on the bulkhead into the engine bay, above the wading line. Underbody shield, abrasion sleeve and underbody clips are deleted; the cable sees cabin ambient (≤85 °C) instead of exhaust-side heat, so a T3 (125 °C) insulation class suffices. Physics: the cable leaves the splash zone entirely, so IP-rated underbody fixings and heat shielding are no longer required. Benchmark: Land Rover places the MHEV 48 V battery under the boot floor and rates the Defender to wade 900 mm at off-road height — exactly the case in which an underbody 48 V run is at risk.

title: Bidirectional DC-DC pre-charges the 48 V bus from 12 V, deleting battery pre-charge branch
description: [MHEV] Pre-charge MOSFET (€0.8-1.0), power resistor(s) and pad (€0.8-1.5), driver/diagnostic channel (€0.6-0.8) and PCB area (€0.3-0.5) deleted; adds DC-DC firmware state and a CAN signal only. Baseline: before the 48 V battery main switch closes, the DC-link capacitors of the starter-generator inverter, DC-DC and other 48 V consumers (typically 3-8 mF in total) must be charged to near battery voltage to avoid an inrush of several kA. 48 V batteries therefore usually carry a pre-charge branch: a 100 V pre-charge MOSFET, a 5-10 W pre-charge resistor (or two in series), its heatsinking pad, and a separate gate driver and diagnostic channel on the BMS power section. Proposal: the 48 V/12 V DC-DC converter is bidirectional and can boost from the 12 V side; at wake-up, the vehicle energy manager commands the DC-DC into boost mode with a current limit of ~10-20 A until the 48 V bus is within 2 V of the battery voltage (reported by the BMS over CAN), then the battery switch closes. Pre-charge time: 6 mF × 48 V / 15 A ≈ 19 ms, invisible to the driver. The pre-charge MOSFET, resistor, its driver and its diagnosis are deleted from the battery. For the rare case that the 12 V side is flat, the battery switch falls back to a pulsed (PWM-limited) closing of the main MOSFETs within their SOA. Benchmark: 48 V/12 V DC-DC converters are bidirectional with synchronous switches allowing boost mod

title: Hook-in rails moulded on 48 V battery housing replace stamped steel cradle
description: [MHEV] Stamped cradle with weld nuts and e-coat (€6-9), 2-4 bolts (€0.3-0.6) and one bolting operation (≈60 s) deleted; compression limiters, hook features and body studs added (€1.5-2.0). Baseline: a 48 V battery of 8-12 kg under the boot floor is typically seated in a stamped steel cradle (DC04 or HX340LAD, 1.5 mm, e-coated, with 4 weld nuts) bolted to the body with 4 M8 bolts, the battery then bolted into the cradle with another 2-4 bolts. Proposal: mould two hook rails at the rear of the PP-LGF30 housing that engage two body-mounted M8 weld studs with flanged spacers, and two front feet with pressed-in steel compression limiters (EN 10277 11SMnPb30-free 11SMn30, 13 mm OD) for 2 M8 bolts straight into body weld nuts. The cradle is deleted. Load check: a 12 kg battery under a 30 g crash pulse gives 3.5 kN, shared by two hooks and two bolts; PP-LGF30 at the hook section (~120 mm² shear area, ~40 MPa shear) carries ≈4.8 kN per hook, and the bolts carry clamp load through the steel limiters so the polymer does not creep. For off-road duty the body-mounted vibration profile (ISO 16750-3) is extended with rough-road shock pulses. Benchmark: Land Rover places the MHEV 48 V battery under the boot floor and Mercedes uses a rear-mounted 0.9 kWh battery — compact units that can be carried directly on the body.

title: 48 V main cable sized to boost duty cycle: 25 mm² replaces 35-50 mm²
description: [MHEV] Copper reduction of 10 mm² over ~5 m (0.45 kg Cu) on the positive run (and on the negative where a return cable exists), smaller lugs and lighter fixings. Baseline: 48 V main cables between battery, starter-generator and DC-DC are often sized for continuous current at the peak machine rating, giving 35-50 mm² copper (supplier 48 V eyelet connectors are offered for 50-70 mm² and rated 240 A at 111 °C on 50 mm²). Proposal: size by transient thermal duty cycle instead. Boost is time-limited (16 kW for ~10 s gives 333 A at 48 V), while continuous generation is ~4-5 kW (≈100 A). For 25 mm² Cu (0.727 mΩ/m, 0.223 kg/m copper): a 10 s 333 A pulse heats the conductor adiabatically by 333² × 0.000727 × 10 / (0.223 × 385) ≈ 9.4 K, and 100 A continuous sits well within the T3 (125 °C) rating at 85 °C ambient. Voltage drop over 5 m at 333 A is 1.2 V (2.5% of 48 V), acceptable inside the ISO 21780 operating band. The BMS enforces the duty cycle (boost energy limit already exists for battery reasons) and a cable temperature model. Benchmark: Mercedes EQ Boost delivers 16 kW / 250 Nm boost, and 48 V needs a quarter of the 12 V current so wiring can be thinner; 48 V is credited with smaller cable cross-sections across the 4+ km of high-end vehicle wiring.

title: Sealed touch-safe eyelet housings at 48 V terminals replace lug, boot and cover stack
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Per joint: boot (€1.0-1.2), touch cover (€0.7-0.9), sealant heat-shrink (€0.8-1.0), and ~45 s of fitting labour deleted; offset by the eyelet-housing premium over a bare lug (€2.0-2.5). Field corrosion repairs after wading reduced. Baseline: 48 V high-current joints at the starter-generator B+, battery post and DC-DC input are typically a tin-plated tubular ring lug on an M8 stud, a separately fitted EPDM boot, a hinged PA6 touch cover and, on underbody or engine joints, a sealant or adhesive-lined heat-shrink to stop wicking — four parts and three operations per joint, and the most common corrosion site after wading. Proposal: one sealed eyelet connector housing per joint (PBT-GF30 or PA66-GF30, integral cable seal and face seal, integrated touch-safe cap with CPA), crimped at the harness supplier; at the vehicle, one bolt and one click. Sealing reaches IP67/IP6K9K, covering 900 mm wading and pressure washing; the face seal stops water reaching the stud. Physics: water ingress at bolted lugs follows the cable strands by capillary action; a seal on the insulation plus a face seal on the stud boss removes both paths. title: Hot-plate welded PP-LGF30 lid replaces EPDM gasket and twelve screws on 48 V battery
description: [MHEV] EPDM gasket (€2.5-3.5), 12 screws and inserts (€1.8-2.4), screw-station labour (€0.8) and leak-test rework (€0.4-0.6) deleted; hot-plate welding adds €0.9-1.2 per unit (machine amortisation, energy). Baseline: a 48 V battery housing is closed with a die-cut or moulded EPDM gasket in a groove and 10-14 self-tapping screws or screws into brass inserts, followed by a pressure-decay leak test; gasket compression set and screw torque scatter are the usual leak-test rejects. Proposal: with a PP-LGF30 tray and lid, close the housing with a hot-plate (or infrared) weld: a 2.5 mm weld rib on the lid, 1.5 mm melt-down, 45-55 s machine cycle, giving a hermetic, monolithic joint with ≥80% of parent-material tensile strength. Gasket, screws and inserts are deleted; the pressure-equalisation function moves to a membrane vent (see separate vent idea). Physics: PP-to-PP welds are diffusion joints with no ageing seal; hermeticity no longer depends on clamp load, so the lid can be thinner between bosses. Service strategy: 48 V batteries are replaced as a unit; the welded lid makes that explicit, and the cut-open procedure for recycling is defined (saw line moulded in). Benchmark: Mercedes uses a compact rear-mounted 0.9 kWh 48 V battery and Land Rover locates its 48 V battery under the boot floor — enclosed, low-energy units suited to a non-serviceable sealed housing.

title: Stainless strapping bands with moulded end blocks replace aluminium end plates on 14s stack
description: [MHEV] Two aluminium end plates (€3.5-5.0 incl. machining) and tie rods/side straps (€1.5-2.0) replaced by two moulded blocks (€1.2-1.6) and two bands with seals (€0.5-0.7); welding/rundown replaced by a strapping head. Baseline: a 13-14-cell prismatic stack in a 48 V battery is compressed between two EN AW-6082-T6 machined or extruded aluminium end plates (≈8-12 mm), tied by two laser-welded steel side straps or four M6 tie rods, assembled in a hydraulic press with a welding or rundown operation. Proposal: two injection-moulded PA66-GF50 end blocks (with ribbed back face and integral busbar-carrier datum features) and two 0.6 × 20 mm stainless steel bands 1.4310 (X10CrNi18-8, Rm ≈1,300 MPa cold-rolled) tensioned and sealed with a crimped seal or laser-tacked overlap — the strapping principle used in packaging. LFP cells need modest, sustained compression (end-of-life swelling small compared with NMC): the band load is set by the press at 4-6 kN; band strain at 6 kN is 6,000 / (0.6 × 20) = 500 MPa, about 40% of tensile strength, leaving margin for swelling and creep. Physics: the moulded end block distributes the load via ribs; a stainless band has no relaxation at <85 °C. Benchmark: Audi's 48 V unit is a ~13-cell 10 Ah stack and Mercedes uses a 0.9 kWh pack — small stacks where the end-plate mass is a large share of the structure.

title: Jump-start post feeds DC-DC boost only: 25 mm² replaces 50 mm² jump cable
description: [MHEV] 25 mm² less copper over 4.5 m (≈1.0 kg Cu), smaller lugs and fuse at the post; no added hardware because the DC-DC boost mode and current limit already exist. Baseline: luxury SUVs with the 12 V battery in the boot or under the floor carry an under-bonnet remote jump-start post connected by a ~4.5 m, 50 mm² copper cable, sized to carry 12 V starter cranking current (300-600 A) from a donor vehicle. Proposal: on MHEV variants where every start (including cold start) is done by the 48 V starter-generator and no 12 V starter is fitted, an external jump only needs to (a) wake the 12 V ECUs and (b) recharge a depleted 48 V battery through the DC-DC converter in boost mode, which current-limits its 12 V input to ~100 A (1.2 kW). Size the jump cable to 25 mm² (100 A continuous within T3 limits, 4.5 m × 0.727 mΩ/m = 3.3 mΩ → 0.33 V drop) with a 125 A protection fuse at the post. The DC-DC boost procedure then raises the 48 V battery to a start-capable SOC in a few minutes before the 48 V machine cranks. Benchmark: in the Mercedes GLE (V167) 48 V system the 12 V battery can charge the 48 V battery through the internal converter in a "starting assistance" procedure; EQ Boost's ISG eliminates the separate starter; 48 V/12 V DC-DC converters are bidirectional with boost capability.

title: Busbar and sense carrier in halogen-free PP-GF20 V-0 replaces PC/ABS V-0 moulding
description: [MHEV] Lower resin price per kg and ~5-8% lower part mass at equal volume; same tool concept (new tool or re-cut for PP shrinkage). Savings are piece-price and labour; engineering cost is treated as one-off and excluded. Baseline: the injection-moulded carrier on top of a 14s prismatic 48 V stack that locates the 13 interconnects, the two terminal busbars and the cell-voltage sense tabs, and insulates them from the housing lid, is commonly PC/ABS UL94 V-0 (density ~1.18-1.20 g/cm³, ~140-180 g part). Proposal: a halogen-free flame-retardant PP-GF20 compound rated UL94 V-0 at 1.5 mm (density ~1.10-1.15 g/cm³), with walls kept ≥1.5 mm at flame-relevant sections and ribs for stiffness. At 48 V (≤58 V) the carrier needs only basic creepage (a few mm) and a CTI of ≥400 V, which PP compounds meet comfortably (CTI typically 600 V class), so the higher-performance PC/ABS is over-specified; the carrier sits in a sealed housing with a maximum service temperature of ~85 °C, well within PP-GF20 HDT. The housing (PP-LGF30) and carrier become the same polymer family, simplifying end-of-life separation, and the carrier's top wall is extended to replace the separate PET insulation sheet under the lid. title: EN AW-1050A busbars with thinned weld lands replace nickel-plated Cu-ETP in 48 V string
description: [MHEV] Per busbar: copper strip plus nickel plating (≈€0.50-0.60) replaced by stamped aluminium (≈€0.15-0.20); weld yield improves by removing the dissimilar joint. Baseline: the 13 series interconnects of a 14s 48 V battery are often nickel-plated Cu-ETP (CW004A) strips, ~2 × 20 mm × 40 mm, laser-welded to the cell terminals; on LFP prismatic cells with aluminium terminals (positive Al, negative Cu-Al composite with Al face), Cu-to-Al is a dissimilar laser weld prone to brittle intermetallics. Proposal: EN AW-1050A-H14 aluminium busbars, 3 × 20 mm (60 mm² section, equal resistance to ~37 mm² copper), stamped with coined/thinned weld lands of 1.0-1.2 mm at the terminal so a single-mode fibre laser (1.5-2 kW, wobble) produces a full-penetration Al-Al weld, while the body keeps its full section. Mass per busbar falls from ~14.3 g Cu to ~6.5 g Al; nickel plating disappears. Physics: Al-Al welds avoid Cu-Al intermetallics, giving more stable joint resistance; the 60 mm² Al section carries 330 A peak at 5.5 A/mm². Benchmark: a published patent (CN114388986A) describes laser-welded battery busbars with welding surfaces thinner than the rest of the conductor for effective welding.

title: Moulded-in PP-LGF30 terminal shroud replaces separate PA6 touch cover on 48 V battery
description: [MHEV] Two PA6 covers with tethers (€0.5-0.7 each), the warning label on the cover (€0.10) and two fitting operations (≈20 s) deleted; mould change cost amortised over volume. Baseline: the 48 V battery positive terminal (M8 stud) is protected by a separate hinged or clip-on PA6 touch-protection cover with a tether, plus a 48 V warning label on the cover; the negative/ground stud uses a second cover. Proposal: mould the shroud into the PP-LGF30 lid — a 25 mm high wall around each stud with a slot for the sealed eyelet housing, so that with the eyelet housing fitted (see sealed eyelet idea) the joint is finger-safe (IP2XB, test finger per IEC 60529) without any separate cover; the 48 V marking is moulded in relief. Physics: the shroud only needs to block the test finger and act as a creepage barrier (58 V needs only a few mm under DIN EN 60664-1); the PP-LGF30 lid already has the stiffness. Benchmark: 48 V connector systems treat touch safety as a core requirement (first-mate/last-break, CPA), and are designed with creepage per DIN 60664-1 — requirements the shroud plus eyelet housing meets together.

title: Laser-marked DataMatrix and hazard symbols on battery housing replace four printed labels
description: [MHEV] Labels (€0.30-0.40 each × 4), ribbon and applicator maintenance deleted; additive (€0.15) and laser cycle (€0.15-0.20) added. Savings are piece-price and labour; engineering cost is treated as one-off and excluded. Baseline: a 48 V battery carries 3-5 polyester (PET) labels — a thermal-transfer-printed type plate with serial number and DataMatrix, a 48 V/electrical hazard label, a recycling/chemistry label and often a separate EOL test pass label — applied by an automatic label applicator and verified by a code reader. Proposal: add a laser-marking additive masterbatch (~0.5-1% by weight) to the black PP-LGF30 lid and mark serial DataMatrix (ECC200, ISO/IEC 15415 grade B or better), hazard symbols, chemistry and recycling marks directly with a 20 W fibre laser at the EOL station (≈6-8 s). The EOL pass state is written to the BMS and the traceability database instead of a sticker. Physics: the additive absorbs at 1,064 nm and foams/carbonises the surface, giving a light-on-dark mark that survives heat, oil and abrasion better than a PET label adhesive. Benchmark: Mercedes and Land Rover place their 48 V batteries in the rear/under the boot floor, where labels must survive service handling — and EU battery rules increasingly require durable marking.

title: Battery main switch: 3+3 TOLL-packaged 100 V MOSFETs replace 4+4 D2PAK-7 devices
description: [MHEV] Two fewer MOSFETs and their gate resistors, plus smaller board area: 8 × €1.60 = €12.80 vs 6 × €1.80 = €10.80, plus ~10 cm² of heavy-copper board and placement. Baseline: a back-to-back 48 V battery main switch built from 100 V MOSFETs in D2PAK-7 (TO-263-7): typically 4 + 4 in parallel at ~1.8 mΩ each, giving ~0.45 mΩ per direction and ~0.9 mΩ total, soldered on heavy copper with large pads for heat spreading. Proposal: 3 + 3 MOSFETs in TOLL (TO-Leadless, ~10 × 11.7 mm, ~30% smaller footprint, lower package resistance and inductance) at ~1.2 mΩ class, giving 0.4 mΩ per direction and 0.8 mΩ total — equal or lower losses (330 A peak: 0.8 mΩ × 330² ≈ 87 W for seconds; 100 A continuous ≈ 8 W). TOLL's exposed pad and gull-wing leads suit thermal-via cooling and AOI inspection. Physics: package resistance and source inductance fall with leadless packaging, so fewer devices meet the same R_DS(on) total and current-sharing improves. Benchmark: 48 V nets require semiconductor components rated 80 V or more on the 48 V side (100 V class used here, covering the 58 V upper dynamic limit of LV 148), and BMW and Mercedes MHEVs both rely on dedicated 48 V battery disconnect devices.
