title: Combined ePTFE breather and burst disc, heat-staked into lid, replaces two vents
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Breather plug with O-ring (€1.2-1.6) and separate rupture valve (€1.5-2.2) replaced by one combined heat-staked vent (€1.0-1.4); boss features and two assembly operations deleted. Baseline: a sealed 48 V battery carries a screw-in PA66 breather plug with O-ring and ePTFE membrane for pressure equalisation, plus a separate rupture disc or spring vent valve for a cell venting event, each needing a machined or moulded boss, an O-ring and a torque or click operation. Proposal: one heat-staked (or ultrasonically welded) combined vent: an ePTFE membrane (IP68 rated, ~1-2 l/h airflow at 7 kPa) bonded on a PP carrier ring that also acts as a burst element, opening at ~20-40 kPa to release cell gas. LFP cells release relatively small gas volumes, which a 10-15 mm opening handles. The vent sits on the top face, above the battery's own splash zone. Physics: when a hot battery is suddenly cooled — e.g. by wading water reaching an under-boot battery tray — the housing internal pressure drops by several kPa; without equalisation, the seal is loaded in vacuum and water can be drawn in. The membrane equalises pressure while blocking liquid water. Benchmark: Land Rover locates the MHEV 48 V battery under the boot floor and rates the Defender for 900 mm wading — the case where breathing without water ingress matters.

title: DC-DC mounting frame clamps 12 V battery base ledge, deleting steel hold-down bar
description: [MHEV] Hold-down bar (€1.2-1.6), two J-bolts and nuts (€0.4-0.6) and one bolting operation (≈30 s) deleted; clamp feet added to the DC-DC frame (€0.3-0.5). Savings are piece-price and labour; engineering cost is treated as one-off and excluded. Baseline: the 12 V battery in the boot is held by a separate e-coated DC04 steel hold-down bar or top frame (~2 mm) with two M6 J-bolts and nuts, while the 48 V/12 V DC-DC converter beside it has its own bracket. Proposal: where the DC-DC is mounted on or next to the 12 V battery (as in the Audi layout), give the DC-DC mounting frame two clamp feet that bear on the battery's EN 50342-2 base ledges; the frame is a PP-LGF30 moulding (or EN AW-6063-T6 extrusion where it doubles as a heatsink), fixed to the body with the two bolts the DC-DC needs anyway. The separate hold-down bar, J-bolts and nuts are deleted. Load check: a 20 kg AGM battery under a 20 g longitudinal pulse needs ~3.9 kN retention, carried by base-ledge clamps (friction + positive ledge engagement) and the frame's two M8 bolts. Physics: the base ledge is the standard EN battery retention feature, so no battery change is needed. Benchmark: in the Audi 48 V system the DC-DC converter sits on top of the 12 V battery in the rear luggage compartment.

title: 48 V rack EPS for the 2.7 t SUV cuts supply current fourfold
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Money comes from the heavy 12 V EPS feed (35 mm² → 6 mm², 3 m, plus 150 A fuse → 40 A), halving the MOSFET count in the bridge, a smaller DC-link and motor copper, and deleting the 12 V voltage-stabilisation buffer where the EPS was the reason it was fitted; offset by a 48 V-rated connector and 12 V logic supply retention. Baseline: a 2.6-2.8 t luxury SUV with 1,450-1,600 kg front axle load runs a 12 V axis-parallel (APA) rack EPS with 16-18 kN rack force. The motor needs ~1.0-1.2 kW at full-lock dry parking, so the ECU draws 100-120 A battery current (phase peaks ~150 A), fed by a dedicated 25-35 mm² cable and 125-150 A fuse from the 12 V battery, with 12 paralleled MOSFETs in the bridge and, on many heavy vehicles, a 12 V voltage-stabilisation buffer to stop lamp/infotainment dips during parking manoeuvres. Proposal: keep the rack, ball-nut and belt reduction unchanged, rewind the EPS motor for 48 V (≈4× turns at ¼ conductor area), run the bridge from the 48 V rail with six 100 V MOSFETs and supply it through a 4-6 mm² feed from the 48 V distribution; logic and the redundant wake/CAN path stay on 12 V. Physics: I = P/V, so 1.2 kW draws ~27 A at 48 V instead of ~110 A at 12 V; I²R loss in a 3 m feed falls 16× at equal cross-section, which also means no thermal derating during long full-lock crawl or nose-heavy towing manoeuvres. Benchmark: Bosch markets EPSap

The motor needs ~1.0-1.2 kW at full-lock dry parking, so the ECU draws 100-120 A battery current (phase peaks ~150 A), fed by a dedicated 25-35 mm² cable and 125-150 A fuse from the 12 V battery, with 12 paralleled MOSFETs in the bridge and, on many heavy vehicles, a 12 V voltage-stabilisation buffer to stop lamp/infotainment dips during parking manoeuvres. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Money comes from the heavy 12 V EPS feed (35 mm² → 6 mm², 3 m, plus 150 A fuse → 40 A), halving the MOSFET count in the bridge, a smaller DC-link and motor copper, and deleting the 12 V voltage-stabilisation buffer where the EPS was the reason it was fitted; offset by a 48 V-rated connector and 12 V logic supply retention.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Same rack assembly line; only the motor winding programme (more turns, thinner wire, same lamination stack) and the ECU power-stage SMT program change. Harness loses one heavy-gauge crimp station (35 mm² ultrasonic weld); no new capex beyond EOL tester 48 V supply (~€60k).
ideaData.dfmDfa: One less heavy cable routed through the engine bay and bulkhead grommet; 48 V connector is keyed differently from the 12 V EPS connector so 12 V and 48 V racks cannot be cross-fitted. Service: rack swap unchanged; 48 V touch-safe below 60 V DC so no HV training needed.

title: One scroll set and housing for 48 V MHEV and 800 V BEV e-compressors

ideaData.title: One scroll set and housing for 48 V MHEV and 800 V BEV e-compressors
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: a shared MHEV/BEV platform buys two unrelated compressors — on MHEV a 48 V electric scroll (or belt-driven swash-plate) of ~27-30 cc from one supplier family, on BEV an 800 V scroll of ~34 cc from another — so two scroll machining routes, two die-cast housing sets (EN AC-46000), two oil-separator designs and two NVH validation campaigns. Proposal: specify ONE mechanical compressor core — fixed and orbiting scrolls, Oldham ring, crank/bearing set, suction and discharge housings, oil separator — at 30 cc, and vary only the motor winding (48 V low-turn vs 800 V high-turn) and the bolt-on inverter lid. MHEV runs it to ~6,000 rpm within a ~4 kW 48 V current limit; BEV runs it to 8,500-9,000 rpm for battery chilling and fast-charge cooling. Physics: scroll displacement × speed sets refrigerant mass flow, so one geometry spans both duties by speed range; the motor stator stack length is common and only turns/wire size change. Benchmark: Sanden supplied a 48 V electric compressor to the Mercedes S-Class/E-Class mild hybrids, and Hanon Systems builds electric scroll compressors with integrated inverters that fit the old belt-driven package — evidence that the 48 V e-compressor is a mature scroll product whose mechanics need not differ from its HV sibling.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Doubling volume on one scroll machining line and one housing die set cuts piece cost of the mechanical core 6-9%, removes one housing tool set (~€1.2-1.6M) and one supplier validation programme; the MHEV also avoids paying for a bespoke low-volume 48 V mechanical design.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Single scroll milling/finishing line at the supplier (5-axis profile milling ~90 s per scroll pair) shared across both variants; motor winding line runs two programs; inverter lids assembled on the same final-assembly cell with a variant nest. Tooling capex down ~€1.4M.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Identical mounting bolt pattern and refrigerant port positions mean one bracket and one hose-end design across powertrains; the inverter lid is keyed by connector (48 V two-pole vs HV with HVIL) to prevent misbuild. Service parts consolidate to one compressor core.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — volume pooling on the costliest mechanical sub-module

Validate per SAE J639/ISO 13043 refrigerant safety, LV 124 (48 V: LV 148) and 1,000 h durability.

ideaData.title: Diesel I6: 48 V 3 kW PTC air heater replaces fuel-fired warm-up heater
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: an efficient 3.0 L diesel I6 rejects too little heat to coolant at -10 °C to meet a 10-minute cabin warm-up target in a 3-row SUV, so diesel builds typically carry a fuel-fired coolant heater (~5 kW: burner, glow pin, metering pump, fuel tap on the tank, combustion-air intake, exhaust pipe, own ECU) plus a 12 V PTC air booster of only ~1.0-1.5 kW (limited by ~100 A on the 12 V net). Proposal: fit a 48 V PTC air heater of ~3 kW in the HVAC heater pocket, fed from the BiSG-supported 48 V rail during driving and idle, three stages switched by 100 V MOSFETs; the fuel-fired heater becomes a cold-climate option (Nordic/Russia-type markets, parking heating) instead of standard diesel content. Physics: 3 kW at 48 V is 63 A, achievable on the 48 V net, whereas 3 kW at 12 V would need 250 A; air-side PTC heats air directly with no coolant thermal mass to warm first, so the effective first-5-minute heat to the cabin is comparable to a 5 kW coolant heater that must also warm the engine loop. The BiSG supplies ~3 kW at modest fuel penalty while warming the engine via added load. Benchmark: Eberspächer offers low-voltage air heaters in 48 V versions installed in the HVAC unit, and BorgWarner markets PTC air heaters for low-voltage use that clear the windscreen within ~60 s.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deleting the fuel-fired heater, its fuel metering pump, tank tap, exhaust and intake lines (€120-160 on fitted diesels) and the 12 V PTC (€25-30), minus the 48 V PTC (€60-75) nets €85-115 per diesel; at a 40% diesel share of MHEV build that is €34-46 per MHEV vehicle before option-pack complexity (keeping 15% optional take-up).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Removes the under-floor heater installation (burner, fuel line, exhaust routing; ~4 min at the marriage/underbody line) from diesel builds; HVAC module simply receives the 48 V PTC in place of the 12 V one at the Tier-1 — no new station. No fuel-system leak-test added for the heater tap.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count falls by ~18-22 items (heater, brackets, fuel pipes, clamps, exhaust, intake hose, fuses). Same heater-pocket rails for 12 V and 48 V PTC envelopes with keyed connector. Service: no burner coking/glow-pin maintenance.

title: 48 V silver-coated windscreen merges solar control and heating, deletes wire screen
description: [MHEV] Deletes the wire-laying process and the separate solar-control film/coating premium (one coating does both), the 12 V 80 A relay and heavy feed, and lets the HVAC defrost PTC stage be downsized since the screen clears itself; net of the 48 V power switch and busbar. Baseline: luxury SUVs commonly buy two functions in one windscreen: an IR-reflective (solar-control) coated or film laminate AND a wire-heated screen with ~0.02 mm tungsten wires robot-laid into the PVB, supplied at 12 V through a 60-80 A relay and heavy feed (~800-900 W). Wires cause starburst under oncoming lights and limit the heated area. Proposal: one sputtered multi-layer silver coating (~20 layers incl. Ag) on ply 2 or 3 does both — reflects solar IR and acts as the transparent heater — energised at 48 V through printed busbars, PWM-limited to ~1.2-1.5 kW. Physics: P = V²/R. title: Mid-trim de-content: single 48 V roll motor on steer axle, tuned tubular bar aft
description: [MHEV] Removes the rear actuator (motor, three-stage gearbox, sensors, electronics, 48 V feed) on mid trims, replaced by a passive tubular bar and links; also cuts 48 V peak current demand so the 48 V fuse/distribution for chassis drops a size. Baseline: electric active roll control on luxury SUVs (Range Rover Dynamic Response Pro, Audi eAWS, Bentley Dynamic Ride) puts a powered unit on BOTH axles: a 48 V motor plus multi-stage planetary (Audi quotes three stages, up to 1,200 Nm; Bentley ~1,300 Nm) between split bar halves, each with its own electronics and 48 V feed. Proposal for mid-trim MHEV builds: keep the powered unit only on the steered axle, sized for the full roll moment it must carry (~60-65% of total roll stiffness), and on the second axle fit a passive hollow 34MnB5 tube (Ø26 × 4 mm, quenched and tempered, shot-peened) tuned for the remaining ~35-40%. Physics: body roll angle is set by total roll stiffness and the handling balance by how it is split between axles; a powered unit on the steered axle can still vary that axle’s stiffness widely, so the controller shapes the roll gradient (target ≤2.5°/g) and goes soft on one-sided bumps at the nose. What is lost is mainly comfort on one-sided inputs at the second axle and part of the balance authority, which rear-wheel steering and brake torque vectoring partly restore. Top trims keep two powered units. Benchmark: Audi

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: where a mild-hybrid SUV keeps a belt-driven compressor (or carries one over from the non-hybrid engine), engine-off stop-start in hot climates is protected by a cold-storage (latent-heat) evaporator: a brazed evaporator with extra tube rows filled with ~0.4-0.6 kg of paraffin phase-change material that freezes while the compressor runs and releases ~40-60 s of cooling at a stop, plus logic that restarts the engine when the discharge-air temperature rises. The PCM evaporator is ~20-30% heavier and costlier than a plain one and is larger in the HVAC case. Proposal: with a 48 V electric scroll compressor that runs independently of the engine, keep the compressor running through stops, coasting and engine-off sailing; specify a standard two-row brazed evaporator (EN AW-3003/4343, 38 mm depth) without PCM, and delete the engine-restart-for-comfort calibration. Physics: maintaining ~2-3 kW of cooling at a stop needs ~0.8-1.2 kW electrical at 48 V (~20-25 A), which the 48 V battery sustains for several minutes and the BiSG recovers on the next deceleration, whereas the PCM gives only a fixed ~50 kJ buffer. Benchmark: the Mercedes S-Class electric refrigerant compressor keeps climate control working in gliding mode and when stationary with the engine off, and Hanon Systems’ e-compressor cools the cabin with the engine off; Sanden’s 48 V compressor serves those belt-less mild hybrids.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the PCM charge, extra tube rows and fill/seal operation of the cold-storage evaporator, and the larger evaporator pocket in the HVAC case; stop duration is no longer cut short by comfort restarts, adding uncounted fuel benefit. Assumes the 48 V e-compressor is already chosen for other reasons.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: At the evaporator supplier the PCM filling, sealing and leak test (~45 s, separate station) disappear; standard evaporator runs on the existing brazing line. HVAC case keeps one evaporator pocket size across MHEV and BEV.
ideaData.dfmDfa: One evaporator part number for MHEV and BEV (BEV never needed PCM); lighter, smaller part simplifies the case and blend-door packaging. Service: no PCM leakage failure mode.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — removes a stop-start crutch
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cold-storage evaporator premium €10-15 (PCM, extra rows, fill/seal) + HVAC case/pocket simplification €1-2 − energy-management calibration amortised €1-2 = €8-14 per vehicle (warm-market share where PCM evaporator was standard averaged in). Range €8-€14 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €400k-€700k/yr.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: 48 V state of charge during long hot idles (traffic in 45 °C) — energy management derates cooling before forcing restart; NVH of the compressor running engine-off (scroll noise audible without engine masking) — mount isolation and speed limit at standstill. Validate with SAE J2765 hot-soak pull-down, stop-start comfort tests at 40-45 °C, and LV 148 energy-balance simulation.

How this differs: Uses that capability to delete the latent-heat cold-storage evaporator still fitted when stop-start comfort relies on PCM.

title: 48 V e-compressor inverter: six 100 V TOLL MOSFETs on IMS, suction-gas cooled
description: [MHEV] Halves MOSFET count, replaces thick-copper FR4 + cold plate + gap pad with one IMS screwed to the existing end cap, and shrinks the DC-link from electrolytic bank to three polymer-hybrid parts. Baseline: a 48 V electric scroll compressor of ~4 kW electrical draws ~85 A DC and ~110-130 A rms phase current. Low-voltage inverters derived from 12 V practice often parallel two D2PAK 80 V MOSFETs per switch (12 devices) on an FR4 board with 4-6 oz copper, bonded to an aluminium cold plate with gap pad, plus a large bank of electrolytic DC-link capacitors (~6-8 × 1,000 µF/63 V). Proposal: one 100 V MOSFET in TOLL (≤1.2 mΩ) per switch, 6 devices total, soldered on an insulated metal substrate (IMS, 1.5 mm Al, 75 µm dielectric) that is screwed directly to the suction-side end cap so returning refrigerant vapour (~0-15 °C) cools it; DC-link becomes 3 × polymer-hybrid capacitors 330 µF/80 V plus film snubber. Physics: TOLL’s lower package resistance and ~0.3 K/W junction-to-case allow a single die per switch at 130 A rms when the heatsink is at refrigerant temperature (~10 °C) rather than under-bonnet air (~105 °C) — conduction loss 130² × 1.2 mΩ ≈ 20 W per conducting switch with ΔTj ~25 K. title: A/C compressor motor at 48 V: tooth-coil 12-slot/8-pole winding for few-turn duty
description: [MHEV] Less copper (~25%) and electrical steel (~10% stack), elimination of multi-strand insertion and end-winding lacing/forming, and higher first-pass yield in winding. Baseline: compressor motors carried over from HV designs use distributed round-wire windings (e.g. 18-slot/6-pole) with long end windings, needle-wound or inserted coils and fill factors ~40-45%. At 48 V and ~4 kW the winding needs only a few turns of large section (≈5-7 turns/coil, ~8-10 mm² per coil conductor), which in round wire means multiple parallel strands that are hard to insert and leave voids. Proposal: a 12-slot/8-pole concentrated (tooth-coil) core with pre-formed edgewise-bent copper coils (Cu-ETP, 1.8 × 5.0 mm, grade-2 polyamide-imide enamel), segmented T-shaped teeth in M330-35A pressed back into a ring, coils slid onto teeth before ring closure; fill factor ~60-65%. End-winding length falls ~40%, copper mass ~25%. Physics: phase resistance R ∝ (turn length)/(fill × slot area); shorter end turns and higher fill lower copper loss at the high currents a 48 V machine runs, allowing the stack length to drop ~10% for the same continuous torque; 12s/8p gives acceptable winding factor (0.866) and low cogging for refrigerant NVH. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Less copper (~25%) and electrical steel (~10% stack), elimination of multi-strand insertion and end-winding lacing/forming, and higher first-pass yield in winding.

title: Actuator-mounted electronics on 48 V roll stabiliser delete shielded phase cables
description: [MHEV] Deletes six shielded phase conductors and sensor cables (two axles), their connectors and EMC ferrites, and the separate ECU housing/bracket; adds a sealed cover and IP6K9K connector on the actuator. Baseline: an electromechanical active roll stabiliser actuator (48 V motor + multi-stage planetary between split bar halves) is often driven from a remote control unit in the body or luggage area, linked by three shielded motor-phase cables (~6-10 mm², 2.5-4 m per axle), plus resolver/position sensor cable and separate 48 V supply — two heavy shielded runs per vehicle crossing the body-to-subframe interface. Proposal: mount the power electronics on the actuator motor end (mechatronic unit): a 6-MOSFET 100 V bridge on IMS sealed in an EN AC-46000 die-cast end cover IP6K9K, with on-axis magnetic angle sensor replacing the cabled resolver; the actuator then needs only an unshielded 48 V pair + CAN-FD/ wake pair. Physics: moving the PWM switching node next to the motor removes the long radiating phase cables (the main EMC source), so shielding and ferrites go; DC current is ~¼-⅓ of the peak phase current, so the supply wire is 2.5-4 mm² rather than 6-10 mm² shielded. Benchmark: Audi eAWS (three-stage planetary, up to 1,200 Nm) and Bentley Dynamic Ride (48 V motor + planetary between bar halves) establish the actuator architecture; this integrates its drive electronics onto it.

title: I6 lubrication: sump-mounted 48 V gerotor e-pump deletes chain-driven engine pump
description: [MHEV] Deletes oil-pump chain, sprocket, tensioner/guide, the variable-displacement cam ring, control spring and two-stage solenoid; the e-pump uses a simple fixed gerotor. Fuel saving (~1-1.5% WLTP, estimated) is a benefit not counted in piece cost. Baseline: a 3.0 L I6 uses a chain-driven, two-stage variable-displacement vane oil pump (sintered rotor, cam ring with pivot and control spring, two-stage control solenoid, chain, tensioner and sprocket) sized for hot idle at 120 °C oil, so at high speed it over-delivers and the excess is throttled or controlled away. Proposal: a 48 V BLDC-driven gerotor oil pump (~700-900 W peak, ~400 W typical) bolted to the sump flange, speed-controlled to a pressure map, with no chain drive; oil pressure follows engine demand exactly including pre-lubrication before a BiSG restart. Physics: a mechanical pump’s flow scales with engine speed while demand is roughly flat above 3,000 rpm, so 40-60% of its high-speed hydraulic power is wasted; an e-pump delivers only the needed Δp × Q (e.g. 4 bar × 40 l/min = 270 W hydraulic). At 48 V, 900 W peak is ~19 A, practical where 12 V (75 A) is not. Valeo states 48 V makes it possible to electrify virtually all engine-driven accessories; Valeo electrical oil pumps already operate in transmissions up to 300 W — the engine application is the higher-power step that 48 V enables.

title: Heated catalyst power stage moved into engine ECU, deleting standalone EHC controller

Baseline: a 48 V electrically heated catalyst (EHC, ~2-4 kW heater disc) is commonly switched by a standalone controller/relay box near the battery or in the engine bay: a sealed housing with its own microcontroller, MOSFET bank, current sense, CAN node and 25-35 mm² feed and return to the catalyst, plus a separate fuse. Proposal: the EHC is a resistive load that only needs PWM duty control; put a 100 V MOSFET high-side switch bank (4 × TOLL in parallel, 80 A) and shunt current sense on a small power daughter board inside the engine ECU or the 48 V battery’s distribution module, controlled by the engine ECU that already runs the cold-start strategy. title: Scroll compressor fixed scroll: squeeze-cast A390 near-net replaces forged A4032
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Less aluminium input (no 50% forging scrap to swarf), ~50% shorter 5-axis milling cycle, deletion of the wear coating step; squeeze-cast die cost is amortised over shared MHEV+BEV volume. Baseline: fixed scrolls of automotive electric compressors are commonly hot-forged from hypereutectic-free A4032 (AlSi12.5MgCuNi) slugs, then the involute wrap is profile-milled from a solid web with ~3-4 mm stock on each flank, removing ~45-55% of the forging mass, followed by anodising or tin-free coating for wear. Proposal: squeeze-cast (indirect, ~100 MPa) fixed scroll in A390 (AlSi17Cu4Mg), primary-silicon refined with P, T6 treated, with the wrap cast to within 0.8-1.0 mm of finish; machine only the flanks and tip faces. Physics: A390’s primary Si (~10-12% volume) gives wrap-flank wear resistance comparable to anodised A4032 without coating, and squeeze casting provides near-zero porosity needed for the thin (~3-4 mm) wraps under ~25 bar differential (R1234yf) or higher for R744; reduced stock cuts milling time roughly in half. Applies to both the 48 V MHEV and the 800 V BEV compressors when the mechanical core is common. Benchmark: production e-scroll compressors from Hanon and Sanden (48 V for Mercedes S/E-Class) confirm the scroll architecture; the material route is a generic proposal.

title: 48 V EPS ECU DC-link: three polymer-hybrid capacitors replace eight 12 V electrolytics
description: [MHEV] Capacitor content falls from ~€4-6 to ~€1.5-2; THT/selective-solder step and adhesive staking for vibration removed; PCB area shrinks ~15 cm², allowing a smaller ECU housing. Baseline: a 12 V heavy-SUV EPS ECU carrying ~110 A DC and ~150 A phase peaks typically uses 6-10 aluminium electrolytic capacitors (e.g. 2,200 µF/25 V, 12.5 × 25 mm, through-hole or SMD with heavy vibration fixing) to absorb ripple current of ~40-60 A rms and hold the bus within ~0.5 V. Proposal: with the motor rewound for 48 V (see the 48 V EPS assembly idea), ripple current falls to ~10-15 A rms and the permissible ripple voltage at the same 3-4% rises to ~1.5-2 V; use three conductive-polymer-hybrid capacitors (e.g. 220 µF/80 V, 10 × 10.5 mm SMD, ~2.5 A rms each at 125 °C) plus a 4.7 µF/100 V MLCC snubber per half-bridge. Physics: required capacitance C ≈ I_ripple / (f_sw × ΔV); with I down 4× and ΔV up 4×, C falls ~16× (from ~15,000 µF to ~700-1,000 µF); polymer-hybrid parts carry the ripple current with low ESR, longer life (no electrolyte dry-out) and SMD reflow instead of THT. Benchmark: Bosch EPSapa highload serves heavy off-road SUVs at 12 V; the 48 V supply move is the enabler and these are its part-level consequences.

title: Roll-actuator first and second planetary stages in sinter-hardened Astaloy 85Mo
description: [MHEV] Removes hobbing, shaving, carburising and bore grinding on 8-10 small gears per actuator; material utilisation ~95% vs ~55% from bar/forging; one heat-treatment step integrated in sintering. Baseline: the three-stage planetary in an electromechanical roll stabiliser (Audi quotes a three-stage planetary; output up to 1,200 Nm; Bentley ~1,300 Nm) is typically made of hobbed and shaved 20MnCr5 or 18CrNiMo7-6 gears, case-carburised (Eht 0.4-0.6 mm), with ground bores — all three stages. Torque at the first stage is only ~1/50-1/80 of the output (≈15-25 Nm), and at the second stage ~1/8-1/10 (≈120-150 Nm). Proposal: make the sun and planet gears of stages 1 and 2 (typically 2 suns + 6-8 planets) as press-and-sinter parts in Astaloy 85Mo + 0.3% C + 2% Cu, density ≥7.15 g/cm³ (warm-compacted), sinter-hardened in the sintering furnace with accelerated cooling (no separate carburising), then steam-treated or shot-peened at the root; keep stage 3 in carburised 18CrNiMo7-6. Physics: PM gear bending fatigue at 7.15+ g/cm³ sinter-hardened reaches ~60-70% of wrought carburised steel, ample for stages loaded at 10-15% of the final stage; net-shape teeth (ISO 8-9 quality) are adequate for low-speed actuator duty where NVH is masked by the bar itself. Benchmark: Audi eAWS and Bentley Dynamic Ride use motor + multi-stage planetary between bar halves; we do not claim their gear materials.

title: Heated-catalyst electrode: MgO-insulated sheathed pin replaces brazed ceramic feedthrough
description: [MHEV] Deletes vacuum active-metal brazing and its leak-scrap, replaces a machined Kovar sleeve and ceramic with continuously produced MI cable cut to length; laser weld replaces TIG with lower distortion. Baseline: the electrode that carries 60-80 A at 48 V into an electrically heated catalyst heater disc through the 1.4512/1.4509 can typically uses an Al2O3 ceramic insulator active-metal-brazed (Ag-Cu-Ti) to a 1.4828 pin and to a Kovar/stainless sleeve, then TIG-welded into the shell — a vacuum-brazing batch step with ~2-4% leak scrap, and a hermetic joint stressed by 900 °C thermal cycling. Proposal: a mineral-insulated sheathed electrode: 1.4767 (FeCrAl) or nickel 201 centre conductor Ø4 mm in compacted MgO powder inside a 1.4841 sheath (Ø8 mm), swaged to density, end sealed with glass-ceramic, and laser-welded directly into the can; the inner end is resistance-welded to the heater disc tab. Physics: compacted MgO has high resistivity at 900 °C (≥10⁶ Ω·cm, ample at 48 V — the issue is only leakage to ground well below insulation-monitoring thresholds) and tolerates thermal shock because the sheath carries mechanical load; swaged MI construction is the proven route of glow plugs and exhaust thermocouples at the same temperatures. 48 V is the enabler: at ≤60 V no creepage/HV insulation rules beyond basic insulation apply. Benchmark: 48 V multi-kW loads on production SUV 48 V

title: 48 V PTC air heater fins: clamped AA1050 corrugated fins replace brazed AA3003
description: [MHEV] Removes the CAB brazing furnace pass (energy, flux, fixtures) and the higher-cost clad alloy; AA1050 strip is cheaper than clad 3003/4343; scrap from braze defects (~1.5-2%) disappears. Baseline: PTC air-heater blocks are often built as brazed assemblies — AA3003 louvred fins with AA4343 clad brazed (CAB, ~600 °C) to flat aluminium tubes or plates that house the ceramic PTC stones, followed by electrical insulation (Kapton or alumina) and frame assembly in PA66-GF30 or PPS. Proposal: unbrazed spring-clamped stack — corrugated louvred fins in AA1050-H18 (thermal conductivity ~220 vs ~160 W/m·K for 3003) pressed against anodised AA1050 contact plates by stainless 1.4310 spring clips, with the PTC stones (BaTiO3, Curie ~180-220 °C, sized for 48 V) held between plates by silicone-free thermal paste; frame PA66-GF30 retained. Physics: heat transfer from stone to air is limited by the stone–plate interface, which spring contact with paste handles at ~2-4 kPa preload; fin-to-plate contact resistance increases slightly, but higher fin conductivity of AA1050 offsets it, keeping block output within ~3% at the same airflow. At 48 V, the stone count for ~3 kW is set by voltage rating rather than current, so each heating register is narrower and carries fewer fins, making clamped construction mechanically easy. Benchmark: Eberspächer offers 48 V low-voltage air heaters and BorgWarner

ideaData.title: 48 V PTC air heater fins: clamped AA1050 corrugated fins replace brazed AA3003
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: PTC air-heater blocks are often built as brazed assemblies — AA3003 louvred fins with AA4343 clad brazed (CAB, ~600 °C) to flat aluminium tubes or plates that house the ceramic PTC stones, followed by electrical insulation (Kapton or alumina) and frame assembly in PA66-GF30 or PPS. Proposal: unbrazed spring-clamped stack — corrugated louvred fins in AA1050-H18 (thermal conductivity ~220 vs ~160 W/m·K for 3003) pressed against anodised AA1050 contact plates by stainless 1.4310 spring clips, with the PTC stones (BaTiO3, Curie ~180-220 °C, sized for 48 V) held between plates by silicone-free thermal paste; frame PA66-GF30 retained. Physics: heat transfer from stone to air is limited by the stone–plate interface, which spring contact with paste handles at ~2-4 kPa preload; fin-to-plate contact resistance increases slightly, but higher fin conductivity of AA1050 offsets it, keeping block output within ~3% at the same airflow. At 48 V, the stone count for ~3 kW is set by voltage rating rather than current, so each heating register is narrower and carries fewer fins, making clamped construction mechanically easy. Benchmark: Eberspächer offers 48 V low-voltage air heaters and BorgWarner PTC air heaters for low-voltage use; their internal construction is not claimed here.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes the CAB brazing furnace pass (energy, flux, fixtures) and the higher-cost clad alloy; AA1050 strip is cheaper than clad 3003/4343; scrap from braze defects (~1.5-2%) disappears.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Continuous fin rolling + stack + spring-clip assembly (~25 s per block) instead of fixture loading, brazing (~20 min furnace transit) and unloading; plant footprint and furnace capex (~€2M) avoided at the supplier.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Clips are symmetric so orientation cannot be wrong; stones replaceable in service only as whole block (unchanged). Paste dispensed by robot to fixed bead.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — process step removed
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: PTC block €30-38: braze/flux/energy −€1.5-2.5 + clad-alloy premium −€1-1.5 + scrap −€0.5-1 = €3-5 per vehicle (48 V PTC standard on MHEV). Range €3-€5 × 50,000 MHEV vehicles/yr = €150k-€250k/yr.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: preload relaxation over thermal cycles leading to stone hot spots; fin vibration noise at high blower speed; corrosion of unbrazed contacts in humid HVAC. Validate with 10,000 thermal cycles, ISO 16750-3 vibration, salt-fog 240 h, and heater output at -20 °C per OEM HVAC spec.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Eberspächer 48 V air heaters; BorgWarner PTC Air Heater — 48 V PTC air heaters installed in the HVAC module.. How this differs: Specifies an unbrazed clamped fin stack in AA1050 for the 48 V heater; does not claim either supplier’s design.

title: Rear-steer actuator push rod: friction-welded C45 tube replaces solid 42CrMo4 bar
description: [MHEV] Material input falls ~35-40% (tube instead of solid bar); long turning operations from bar are replaced by short friction welding of cold-forged ends; induction-hardened volume shrinks with the thinner wall, cutting energy. Baseline: the output push rod of a central rear-steer actuator (11 kN class for vehicles to 3.5 t) is commonly turned from solid 42CrMo4+QT bar (Ø24-28 mm, ~520 mm long), induction-hardened on the bearing/sealing zone, with threaded ends for the tie rods — about 1.9-2.3 kg of material per rod, half removed as chips on reduced sections. Proposal: a precision-welded C45E (1.1191) tube Ø25 × 5 mm, induction-hardened and ground on the seal/bearing zone, with two cold-forged 42CrMo4 end pieces friction-welded on (rotary friction weld, ~8 s each), then thread-rolled. Physics: buckling load F = π²EI/(KL)²; for an Ø25 × 5 tube I is ~87% of a Ø25 solid bar at ~64% of the mass, and the 11 kN axial load with ±5° travel is well within Euler and Johnson limits at an unsupported length ~250 mm (safety factor >4); bending from tie-rod angularity is carried by the 42CrMo4 ends. Weight saving ~0.6-0.8 kg unsprung-adjacent mass. Benchmark: ZF AKC central actuators (Gen 2) reach 11 kN for vehicles up to 3.5 t, the load case we design to; ZF’s rod construction is not claimed.

ideaData.title: Cap 48 V machine at 15 kW; buy remaining CO2 with engine-off sailing calibration
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the next-generation programme brief for a 2.5-2.7 t luxury SUV with 3.0 l I6 typically escalates the 48 V machine from the 12-16 kW class to 20-25 kW "to catch more regen", which drags with it a larger inverter (phase current ~400 A → ~650 A, more 100 V MOSFET dies in parallel), more stator copper and magnet, a 48 V battery up-rated in power (≈0.9 → ≈1.3 kWh class) and a heavier DC cable. Proposal: freeze the machine at 15 kW / ~250 Nm (the class Mercedes uses on its ISG and above the 12 kW of Mazda's CX-60 3.3 l I6 M Hybrid Boost and BMW's 9 kW in the X5 40i 8-speed) and spend the CO2 budget on calibration instead: (1) engine-off sailing between ~55 and 160 km/h with all systems live (Audi runs this on the A8 for up to 40 s), (2) navigation/radar-predictive coast-down that starts sailing or light regen before the driver lifts, (3) engine stop below 22 km/h on approach, (4) regen setpoint shaped to the battery's acceptance rather than the machine's peak. Physics: at 2.6 t a 1.0 m/s² WLTP-type deceleration at 15 m/s demands ~39 kW of braking power, so a bigger machine does capture more in sharp decels, but most WLTP decelerations are short and the 48 V battery acceptance (C-rate, temperature) saturates first; doubling machine power typically buys ~1-2 g/km while sailing and engine-off-on-approach recover a similar amount in real driving at zero BOM cost. The decision rule is explicit: buy hardware only where its € per g/km is below the €95/g/km excess-emissions premium of Regulation (EU) 2019/631.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Avoids the up-rate content: machine (+€55-75 copper, magnet, larger stack), inverter (+€35-50 more MOSFET dies, larger DC-link, bigger busbars) and battery power up-rate (+€60-100), roughly €150-225 per vehicle, while sailing logic is a software cost of ~€1.5M one-off spread over ~250,000 lifetime vehicles (~€6/vehicle).
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: No new tooling: the 15 kW stator/rotor stack, inverter PCB and battery module stay on current lines; the 25 kW up-rate would have required a longer stator stack, new winding fixtures and a new end-of-line test limit set, so ~€2-3M of avoided capex as well.
ideaData.dfmDfa: One machine/inverter/battery power class across all I6 ratings keeps a single part number family, one cooling-jacket interface and one connector; calibration variants live in software datasets selected at end-of-line coding, not in hardware.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — avoids a full power-class step on three 48 V components
costSavingPotential.percentage: 12-18% of the 48 V system (machine + inverter + battery) cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Avoided up-rate €150-225 (machine €55-75 + inverter €35-50 + battery €60-100) minus sailing software €6 and calibration/test €4 ≈ €140-215, taken as €140-210; × 50,000 = €7.0M-10.5M. Valid when the fleet is CO2-compliant; if not, deduct any certified g/km shortfall × €95 per vehicle.

ideaData.riskNotes: Sailing gain in WLTP is smaller than real-world gain; the business case must be scored on the certified WLTP figure plus fleet target position. Validate sailing re-engagement quality (restart and clutch fill <0.5 s), brake vacuum and steering assist during engine-off phases (see sailing vacuum idea), and 48 V battery cycle life (ISO 12405-type cycling) with the higher sailing duty.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Audi A8 (2018, D5) 48 V MHEV; Mazda CX-60 3.3 e-Skyactiv D (2022) — Audi coasts engine-off from 55-160 km/h for up to 40 s on a 12 kW BAS with a 10 Ah battery; Mazda runs its I6 with a 12 kW motor-generator and 0.33 kWh battery.. How this differs: Uses those as proof that a ~12-16 kW class plus strategy delivers the benefit, and formalises a €/g/km gate against the EU €95 premium before any machine up-rate on our I6 SUV.

ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the 12 V variant's engineering, calibration and homologation (~€13M over a 6-year life, ~€2.2M/yr), unique FEAD/front-cover tooling (~€3M, ~€0.5M/yr) and part-number/logistics/plant complexity (€12-18 per vehicle over all 50,000), against ~€1.7M/yr extra kit cost on the low-CO2 markets.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One engine-dress line sequence, one harness family and one EOL route; removes a second FEAD bracket machining operation on the cylinder-head front face and a parallel line-side presentation of starter/alternator.
ideaData.dfmDfa: About 60 unique part numbers fewer; no risk of building a 12 V harness into a 48 V body; single service documentation and diagnostic tree; dealers stock one battery/DC-DC set.

ideaData.riskNotes: Hot-climate markets (GCC, Australia) need 48 V battery thermal validation to 50 °C ambient soak and ISO 16750-4 climatic loads; cold markets need -30 °C start capability on 48 V. If 12 V-only market share grows above ~10%, re-run the arithmetic; price positioning can recover part of the kit cost as performance content.

title: Source 48 V as components with OEM-owned integration and dual-sourced motor-inverter
description: [MHEV] Removes stacked system-integrator margin (6-8% of ~€1,000 = €60-80) and gains 4-6% competitive pricing on the ~€420 motor-inverter package through dual sourcing (€17-25), minus OEM integration cost of €1.5-2.0M/yr (€30-40 per vehicle). Baseline: a 48 V system (machine, inverter, DC-DC, battery, hybrid software) is commonly bought as one turnkey system from a single tier-1, which subcontracts cells, power modules and the DC-DC and adds its own integration margin and risk premium on top (typically 6-10% stacked on a ~€1,000 system), with no competitive pressure after nomination. Proposal: split the system into four component packages with OEM-owned interfaces — (1) machine + inverter (the torque-producing pair) specified by an interface control drawing (stator envelope, spline/hub, coolant ports, 3-phase connector, CAN-FD message catalogue) and nominated to two suppliers at a 70/30 split, (2) DC-DC, (3) 48 V battery with cells sourced by the OEM, (4) hybrid supervisory software owned in-house and hosted on the engine ECU. The system composition is standard enough to package this way: Mazda's CX-60 I6 M Hybrid Boost, for example, is described as battery, inverter, DC/DC converter and motor-generator. A 6-8 person integration team covers system validation, so the margin-on-margin is avoided and the dual-source split keeps annual price-downs competitive.

title: Fold 48 V functional test into roller test; flash 48 V ECUs over DoIP
description: [MHEV] Deletes one EOL station (capex €1.2-1.8M, ~€0.3M/yr over 5 years) and ~3 min of operator/station time per vehicle (at €55/h fully loaded ≈ €2.75), plus fewer CAN flash failures and rework loops. Baseline: four 48 V ECUs (inverter, DC-DC, BMS, hybrid functions) are often flashed and coded at the vehicle EOL over CAN/CAN-FD at a dedicated programming station (4-6 min for the 48 V set), and the 48 V system then gets its own functional test station (battery contactor/MOSFET switch check, DC-DC load step, machine spin and torque plausibility) before the roller dynamometer. Proposal: (1) suppliers deliver ECUs pre-flashed with the series software; the line only writes variant coding and any late delta via DoIP (ISO 13400) through the central gateway, in parallel with the other domain flashes — Ethernet offers 100 Mbit/s-1 Gbit/s against 1-8 Mbit/s for CAN/CAN-FD; (2) the 48 V functional test moves into the roller-test script that already runs the powertrain: during the existing 0-50 km/h cycle the tester commands motor torque steps (±50 Nm) and a regen event, logs DC-DC output under a defined 12 V load and checks the 48 V battery switch, so the stand-alone station disappears. Cycle-time effect ≈3 min of station time and one station footprint deleted per line.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: when the hazard analysis rates "unintended motor torque / unintended regen deceleration" at ASIL C, the 48 V inverter is often developed as the sole ASIL C element: lockstep multicore MCU (high-end safety MCU), redundant phase-current sensing (two sensors per phase or shunt plus Hall), an independent safety supply/watchdog and a separate rotor-position plausibility channel. Proposal: decompose the safety goal per ISO 26262-9 into ASIL B(C) + ASIL A(C): the engine ECU, which already runs an E-Gas-style three-level torque monitor for the combustion engine, adds the electric torque to its level-2 monitoring (compares requested vs estimated total crank torque from DC current × voltage and speed) and owns the safe state; the inverter keeps a simpler ASIL A(C) path — single safety-capable MCU without lockstep, one shunt current sensor per phase with DC-link plausibility, and an active-short-circuit/freewheel shutdown triggered by a hardware path from the ECU. Industry guidance indicates starter-generator circuits are typically ASIL B; this idea makes sure the residual C rating is carried where monitoring is cheapest. Independence between the two elements (separate MCUs, supplies and sensor paths) is demonstrated by dependent-failure analysis.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Smaller inverter control PCB (fewer components, ~10% fewer placements), shorter in-circuit test; no change to EOL beyond a combined torque-plausibility check.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Fewer sensors in the inverter phase busbars simplifies the busbar/sensor assembly, removes a calibration step for redundant sensor matching and frees board area for a smaller control PCB.

title: Spring-piston impulse accumulator replaces electric auxiliary oil pump for sailing re-engagement
description: [MHEV] Electric aux pump assembly €70-100 deleted; accumulator with latch solenoid €15-20 added; net €55-80 per vehicle; also removes a 12 V/48 V load and its driver ECU. Proposal: during engine-off sailing the shift elements are open (neutral) and need no pressure; pressure is needed only for re-engagement, when the 48 V machine spins the transmission input and the input-driven mechanical pump comes up within a few hundred milliseconds. For sailing re-engagement the target gear is pre-selected and the accumulator fills the oncoming clutch while the machine synchronises input speed. title: Delete start-stop voltage stabiliser and ECU boost pre-stages once 12 V never cranks
timeToImplement: 6-12 months (stabiliser); ECU stages at next revision
description: [MHEV] Stabiliser module and installation €22-32 deleted; boost pre-stages in three ECUs €9-15 removed at their next revision; minus DC-DC transient-response verification €1-2 per vehicle. Baseline: 12 V start-stop vehicles protect sensitive loads from the restart dip — the battery can droop below 4 V on cold crank and several volts on warm restarts — using a stand-alone voltage stabiliser (200-400 W boost module with LIN/CAN that bridges up to ~6 s) feeding infotainment, instrument cluster and audio, and/or boost pre-regulators inside those ECUs. Luxury SUVs moving to 48 V often carry these over unchanged. Proposal: when every start is made by the 48 V machine (petrol I6 starter deleted, as in the companion 48 V starter-delete idea) the 12 V net is fed by the DC-DC converter through every restart and never sees a crank dip, so (1) delete the stand-alone stabiliser module (€22-32 with bracket, fuse and harness branch), and (2) on the next ECU revisions specify LV 124 test E-11 (starting profile) with a relaxed functional-status class for the cold-crank profile, removing the input boost stage in infotainment head unit, cluster and amplifier (€3-5 each). The 12 V net still must survive jump-start and load-dump pulses, so input protection stays; only the ride-through-during-crank function goes.

title: Converter kept but one torus size smaller: 48 V fill replaces stall multiplication
description: [MHEV] [Off-road] Smaller impeller/turbine/stator stampings and cover, less steel and brazing, smaller lock-up clutch area: €15-25 per converter; secondary savings in ATF cooling (not counted). Baseline: a luxury SUV towing 3,500 kg and crawling off-road specifies its 8-speed torque converter for launch torque multiplication: a large torus with stall torque ratio ~2.0-2.2 so that the turbo I6 can launch heavily loaded before boost builds. Proposal: retain the torque converter (no change of launch-element concept) but drop one torus size step (≈10-15 mm smaller diameter) and use a stiffer K-factor with stall torque ratio ~1.7-1.8; the 48 V machine adds 200-250 Nm at the transmission input during the first ~1-2 s of launch and during off-road crawl, replacing the lost hydrodynamic multiplication exactly where the turbo has not yet spooled. BMW integrates a 9 kW / 200 Nm 48 V motor in its 8-speed transmission on the X5 40i and Mercedes quotes 250 Nm for its ISG, which is the size of torque this relies on. Off-road: at crawl the machine provides smooth off-idle torque and the low range provides multiplication; a smaller converter also slips less, so ATF heat during low-speed crawling and towing drops, easing the oil cooler. Converter lock-up can start in 1st gear earlier.

title: Sailing-exit rule on stored brake reserve, so engine-off coasting adds no e-pump
description: [MHEV] Electric vacuum pump, bracket, check valve and harness branch (€45-60) deleted; a 0.5 l blow-moulded reservoir (€3-5) added; calibration cost negligible per vehicle. Baseline: an inline-six with a cam-driven mechanical vacuum pump has no brake-assist energy source while the engine is stopped; when engine-off sailing is introduced (Audi coasts engine-off between 55 and 160 km/h for up to 40 s on the A8), programmes typically bolt on a 12 V electric vacuum pump (€45-60 with bracket, check valve, hose and harness) purely to cover the sailing phases. Proposal: make the sailing state machine respect the stored reserve instead of adding a pump. (1) The assist chamber plus a 0.5 l in-line reservoir stores enough for 2-3 full stops from -80 kPa; (2) the existing pressure sensor (already fitted for the ESP hydraulic-assist fallback) is read by the hybrid controller: sailing is not entered below -65 kPa and is terminated — engine restarted by the 48 V machine in ~0.3 s, mechanical pump back on — when the reserve drops below -55 kPa or on the first pedal application above ~0.2 g; (3) the ESP hydraulic assist fallback, already validated for pump failure, remains the backstop. Physics: one full stop uses about 10-15 kPa of reserve, so with ~25 kPa margin the driver always has at least one fully assisted stop before the engine is running again. Calibration cost only; no hardware added

title: Host hybrid supervisory control in engine ECU, deleting the standalone hybrid control unit
description: [MHEV] HCU (€35-50) plus its connector, harness branch and bracket (€6-10) deleted; minus engine ECU flash/RAM derivative upgrade €5-10; one fewer ECU supplier contract and software release stream. Baseline: some 48 V systems are integrated with a dedicated hybrid control unit (HCU) — a separate ECU with its own housing, connector, CAN-FD transceivers, supply and bracket that runs energy management (charge-sustaining strategy, regen/boost split, sailing and stop-start decisions) and talks to the engine ECU, transmission control, BMS, DC-DC and inverter. Proposal: host the hybrid supervisory software as a software component on the engine ECU, which already owns torque coordination and the torque-safety monitor (see ASIL decomposition idea) and in current multicore generations has spare core capacity; the BMS, inverter and DC-DC keep only their device-level control. Benchmark systems are described simply as battery, inverter, DC/DC and motor-generator — Mazda's CX-60 I6 M Hybrid Boost for example — without a separate hybrid ECU being part of the description. Engine ECU memory/core upgrade (if needed) is a cheaper derivative than a whole extra ECU.

title: Starter-delete bell-housing: EN AC-46000 casting without starter pocket and pilot bore
description: [MHEV] Aluminium 0.35-0.45 kg × €3.5/kg (€1.2-1.6) + machining 25-35 s at €1.2/min (€0.5-0.7) + blanking cover and gasket where used (€1.5-2.5) ≈ €3.2-4.8 per housing. Baseline: the transmission bell-housing (EN AC-46000 / AlSi9Cu3(Fe), HPDC, ~8-10 kg) carries a starter pocket with a machined pilot bore (Ø ~76-80 mm, H8), a spot-faced flange, two tapped M12 holes, and a pinion window into the ring-gear zone that needs a blanking cover and seal on any variant without a starter. Proposal: on a starter-less MHEV (48 V machine does all starts, as on Mercedes ISG engines where the ISG replaces starter and alternator), cast the bell-housing with the starter boss and pinion window deleted: closed wall with a 3.0-3.5 mm nominal and a rib in place of the boss. This removes ~0.35-0.45 kg of aluminium, two drilling/tapping operations, the pilot-bore boring and face milling (~25-35 s of 5-axis machining), the blanking cover and its gasket, and a leak path for wading. The die change is an insert swap in the slide that formed the starter pocket.

title: Starter-free 12 V main cable: 50 mm² copper becomes 35 mm² EN AW-1370
description: [MHEV] Copper conductor ~2.0 kg × €9.5/kg (€19) → aluminium ~0.43 kg × €3.2/kg (€1.4); smaller insulation; transition terminals add €3-4; net €14-18 per vehicle. Baseline: with the 12 V battery under the rear loadspace or floor (JLR places its 48 V battery beneath the rear loadspace; 12 V batteries in luxury SUVs are commonly rear-mounted too), the 12 V main cable to the engine bay is sized for starter current (800-1,000 A peak cold crank): ~4.5 m of 50 mm² copper (Cu-ETP, FLRY-type, ~0.45 kg/m conductor). Proposal: once the starter is deleted, the largest 12 V current path is the DC-DC converter output (~3 kW, ≤230 A continuous) and the 12 V battery only buffers; resize to 35 mm² aluminium EN AW-1370 (resistance roughly equal to ~22 mm² Cu: ~0.82 mΩ/m) which keeps voltage drop below 0.4 V at 230 A over 4.5 m, with ultrasonically welded copper-to-aluminium transition terminals (tin-plated Cu-ETP lugs) sealed with adhesive-lined heat-shrink. Cable mass falls from ~2.4 kg to ~0.6 kg. Precondition: this applies only where the 48 V machine makes EVERY start including cold starts — in practice a crank-integrated starter-generator (P1 ISG, as Mercedes uses on the M256 to replace the starter motor and alternator). Belt starter-generator systems commonly keep a 12 V pinion starter for cold starts, so on those builds this idea does not apply.

title: Passive hydromount with decoupler membrane replaces vacuum-switchable engine mounts
description: [MHEV] Switchable mount €55-70 → passive hydromount €32-40, ×2 = €46-60, plus solenoid valve, vacuum hoses and harness branch €6-10; minus calibration of idle active damping (~€1). Baseline: luxury SUVs isolate idle shake with switchable hydromounts — a solenoid or vacuum valve opens an idle inertia track/air chamber to soften the mount at idle and closes it above ~1,200 rpm (Lexus/Toyota/Honda types apply engine vacuum via a solenoid) — two engine mounts at ~€55-70 each plus a solenoid valve, vacuum lines and harness. Proposal: with the 48 V machine stopping the engine at standstill and below ~22 km/h, and starting/stopping it smoothly (Mercedes says its ISG starts the engine faster and more gently than a 12 V starter), the I6 idles far less; residual idle (cold start, A/C pull-down, off-road crawl) is handled by a passive hydromount with a free decoupler membrane and a single inertia track tuned for 8-12 Hz engine bounce damping, plus active 3rd-order damping by the machine at idle. Mount: NR/BR blend 50 ±5 Shore A, ethylene-glycol/water fill, PA66-GF35 housing with crimped steel cup; one part number left/right.

title: Turbo rotor on floating bronze bushes, not ceramic-ball cartridge, as 48 V fills low-end
description: [MHEV] Ball-bearing cartridge (precision races, ceramic balls, cage, damper housing) replaced by two turned bronze bushes and a thrust washer: €30-50 per turbo at the CHRA level, minus a small re-match/calibration cost (~€1-2). Baseline: premium turbo petrol and diesel I6 engines chasing low-end response often specify a ball-bearing turbocharger cartridge — angular-contact duplex bearing with M50 (80MoCrV42-16) races and Si3N4 ceramic balls in a squeeze-film damped cartridge — because it cuts bearing friction at low shaft speed and speeds up spool from part load by roughly 10-20% versus journal bearings; the cartridge costs ≈€30-50 more than a journal-bearing CHRA and needs cleaner oil filtration. Proposal: with a 48 V machine adding 200-250 Nm at the transmission input during the first 1-2 s of a transient (BMW 9 kW / 200 Nm in its 8-speed; Mercedes ISG 16 kW / 250 Nm), the response gap the ball bearing closes is already filled electrically. Revert to a fully floating journal-bearing system — two floating bushes in lead-free CuZn/CuSn bearing alloy (e.g. CuSn8P), a thrust bearing in the same alloy, steel shaft induction-hardened at the journals — with the same compressor/turbine aero. The journal bearing is also more tolerant of the frequent engine-off sailing/stop events (no rolling-element brinelling under vibration while stopped).

title: Starter-free 12 V pre-fuse box: MEGA branch gone, Cu-ETP busbar 3.0 to 1.5 mm
description: [MHEV] Copper busbar mass ~0.12 kg → ~0.06 kg (€0.6), MEGA → MIDI fuse (€2-3), smaller housing and two fewer fuse positions (€2-3), alternator stud/nut deleted (€0.5): €5-7 per vehicle. Baseline: the battery-terminal pre-fuse box (PA66-GF30 housing over a stamped Cu-ETP busbar, 3.0 mm thick, tin-plated) carries the unfused starter branch, a 300-400 A MEGA fuse for the alternator/main feed and 4-6 MIDI fuses; the busbar is sized for starter and alternator current and the box has an alternator stud. Proposal: once the starter and alternator are deleted (the 48 V machine starts the engine and the DC-DC feeds 12 V, as the Mercedes ISG replaces the alternator and starter motor), the highest 12 V current at the box is the DC-DC output (≤230 A) and battery buffering. Redesign the pre-fuse box: delete the starter branch and alternator stud, replace the MEGA by a 250 A MIDI-type fuse, and thin the busbar from 3.0 to 1.5 mm Cu-ETP (CW004A, R240), tin-plated — current density stays under ~10 A/mm² at 230 A on a 25 mm wide section. Box shrinks from 6-way to 4-way. Only for ISG-type builds with no pinion starter; a belt-machine build that keeps a cold-start starter keeps the MEGA branch.

title: 48 V DC cables in unshielded thin-wall T3 insulation, no HV-style orange spec
description: [MHEV] Shielded HV-style cable (~€6-8/m per conductor) → unshielded T3 (~€3-4/m): over ~7-8 m of conductor €18-30; HV-style connectors/shield terminations → sealed stud terminals €6-10; net €20-32 after twisting/bundling cost. Baseline: some 48 V programmes, often driven by supplier carry-over from 400/800 V work, specify the battery-to-inverter and battery-to-DC-DC cables (2 × 35-50 mm², 3-4 m) as shielded, high-voltage-style cables with braided screen, thick-wall XLPE, orange or special colouring and connectors with touch protection and interlock. Proposal: 48 V is voltage class A (below 60 V DC; class B starts above 60 V DC), so no touch protection, HV interlock or orange marking is required; specify unshielded thin-wall copper cable to ISO 6722-1 with T3 (125 °C) cross-linked polyolefin, a distinct colour per OEM 48 V convention, and standard sealed 48 V ring-terminal/stud connections with an arc-safe-disconnect procedure. EMC is handled at the source: inverter and DC-DC carry DC-link filtering, and the positive and return cables are routed as a twisted or tightly bundled pair (loop area <5 cm² per metre) to keep radiated emissions within CISPR 25 class limits. Saves the braid, its termination and the special connectors.

title: Starter-free engine ground strap: 50 mm² tinned copper braid becomes 16 mm²
description: [MHEV] Copper braid 50 mm² → 16 mm² saves ≈0.12-0.15 kg Cu per strap (€1.2-1.5) and lighter ends; deleting the second strap saves another €3-5 including fasteners and assembly (~20 s); total €4-7. Baseline: the engine-to-body (or engine-to-subframe) ground strap is sized for the 12 V starter return current — 800-1,000 A peak at cold crank — typically a 50 mm² tinned Cu-ETP flat braid, 300-450 mm long with pressed and drilled tinned copper ends (M8/M10), often doubled on luxury SUVs with a second strap at the gearbox. Proposal: on starter-free I6 builds (builds where the 48 V machine makes every start, as with the Mercedes ISG replacing the starter motor), the engine ground only returns ECU, sensor, injector, ignition-coil and glow-plug/heater currents of the 12 V net (≤80-120 A peak, a few tens of amps continuous), while the 48 V machine has its own dedicated 48 V return. Re-specify one strap at 16 mm² tinned Cu braid with crimped/pressed ends and delete the second strap; keep an EMC-driven ground (short, wide braid) where RF measurements require it. Voltage drop: 16 mm² × 0.4 m ≈ 0.45 mΩ, i.e. ≈45 mV at 100 A — within ECU ground-offset budgets of ~±1 V (LV 124 E-xx ground offset). Not for builds that keep a 12 V cold-start starter (typical of belt starter-generators): they keep the 50 mm² strap.
